Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a question of privilege relating to the presence within these buildings of armed troops. I do not believe it has ever been necessary in Canadian history to have troops stationed within the precincts of Parliament. I, as a private member, may not be aware, of course, of all that the government may be, but it strikes me as deplorable that armed troops should be within the building. If it were necessary for the protection of members to have additional security within the building, I would not object, but the physical presence of armed troops revolts me.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS WITH PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce the
successful conclusion of our discussions in Stockholm with representatives of the People's Republic of China, reflected in today's joint communique which records our agreement on mutual recognition and the establishment of diplomatic relations. The joint communique of the government of Canada and the government of the People's Republic of China concerning the establishment of diplomatic relations between Canada and China is as follows:
1.	The government of Canada and the government of the People's Republic of China, in accordance with the principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, noninterference in each other's internal affairs and equality and mutual benefit, have decided upon mutual recognition and the establishment of diplomatic relations, effective October 13, 1970.
2.	The Chinese government reaffirms that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the territory of the People's Republic of China. The Canadian government takes note of this position of the Chinese government.
3.	The Canadian government recognizes the government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China.
4.	The Canadian and Chinese governments have agreed to exchange ambassadors within six months, and to provide all necessary assistance for the establishment and the performance of the functions of diplomatic missions in their respective capitals, on the basis of equality and mutual benefit and in accordance with international practice.
Officials from my department and from Industry, Trade and Commerce will be leaving for Peking very shortly to begin administrative preparations for the opening of a Canadian embassy in Peking. We hope to have the embassy in operation within two or three months.
The establishment of diplomatic relations between Canada and China is an important step in the development of relations between our two countries, but it is not the first step, nor is it an end in itself. We have opened a new and important channel of communication, through which I hope we will be able to expand and develop our relations in every sphere. We have already indicated to the Chinese, in our Stockholm discussions, our interest in setting up cultural and educational exchanges, in expand-^
understanding on consular matters,~and in settling a small number of problems left over from an earlier period. The Chinese have expressed the view that our relations in other fields such as these can only benefit from the establishment of diplomatic relations between our two countries. They have also agreed in principle to discuss through normal diplomatic channels, as soon as our respective embassies are operating, some of the specific issues we have raised with them.
As everyone knows, the agreement published today has been under discussion for a long time. I do not think it is any secret that a great deal of this discussion has revolved around the question of Taiwan. From the very beginning of our discussions the Chinese side made clear

October 13, 1970
Recognition of Red China
to us their position that Taiwan was an inalienable part of Chinese territory and that this was a principle to which the Chinese government attached the utmost importance. Our position, which I have stated publicly and which we made clear to the Chinese from the start of our negotiations, is that the Canadian government does not consider it appropriate either to endorse or to challenge the Chinese government's position on the status of Taiwan. This has been our position and it continues to be our position. As the communique says, we have taken note of the Chinese government's statement about Taiwan. We are aware that this is the Chinese view and we realize the importance they attach to it, but we have no comment to make one way or the other.

Mr. Speaker, the members of this party have long urged the recognition of the People's Republic of China by the government of Canada. We are very glad, therefore, that the government of Canada and the government of mainland China have been able to work out the necessary arrangements whereby diplomatic relations can be established between our two countries.
The present government in mainland China has been the de facto government of that vast area for some 21 years, and it seems to be ridiculous to go on failing to recognize the existence of a government which controls almost a quarter of the earth's population. It seems to me that the time was long overdue for taking the step which has now been taken. I am convinced that once diplomatic relations have been established we can work out many cultural exchanges and trading relationships to the mutual advantage of both countries. I believe most Canadians will feel that the step the government has now taken is one which is not only in the interest of Canada but one which could be in the interest of world peace. I say that because I do not think one can long keep a large country such as China out of the councils of the world.
October 13, 1970

With reference to the severing of diplomatic relations with the government or Nationalist China, I would simply point out that when the government in Taiwan is prepared to state that it is the government of that area, and of that area only, it will be time for the Canadian government to negotiate with that government for diplomatic recognition. But as long as the Taiwan government claims to be the government of China, which clearly it is not, it is impossible for the Canadian government to recognize two governments of China. If the government in Formosa should decide to restrict the area over which it claims sovereignty it would then be possible for the Canadian government to discuss with it the question of recognition and the exchange of diplomatic representatives.
I hope that since the government has established, or is in process of establishing, diplomatic relations with mainland China we will now take a much more forthright position with reference to mainland China's entry into the United Nations and her right to sit on the Security Council. I do not think that the United Nations will ever be an effective body for maintaining the rule of law in the world as long as it excludes a country which represents such a vast proportion of the world's population. To have a Security Council composed of the United States, the U.S.S.R., Great Britain, France and Taiwan is ridiculous. I hope that the Canadian government will show some courage at the United Nations by pressing for the admission of China to the United Nations and her right to take her seat on the Security Council of that body.

Trudel for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (p. 29), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) (p. 41).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today at this time it is difficult to come to grips in this speech of mine with the economic problems that face our people. It is also difficult at a time when it would appear that the security and very foundation of our nation are being somewhat shaken. At the outset may I say to the government that now is the time to support to the fullest our administrative personnel and our officers so that law and order can and will be maintained in this nation in the future as it has been in the past.
I might say as an aside that I am confident, and I am sure all members will agree with me, that the majority, more than 99 per cent, of the citizens of Canada, because of being steeped in the traditions of this nation have confidence that we can return soon, I hope, to normalcy. There is an emotional temper afoot. No one can deny that. We saw this today in the question of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and in the Prime Minister's answer to the Leader of the Opposition. I felt that the question and the statement made fitted the responsibility of Parliament in this regard at this time. When one speaks of the emotional temper afoot one cannot help but think of the words of the late president Franklin D. Roosevelt in a statement he made at a time when violence was afoot throughout the world. It is so well put together that it became almost a prayer. This is what he said:
Grant us brotherhood, not only for this day but for all our years-a brotherhood not of words but of acts and deeds. We are all of us children of earth-grant us that simple knowledge. If our brothers are oppressed, then we are oppressed, If they hunger, we hunger. If their freedom is taken away, our freedom is not secure.
Grant us the common faith that man shall know bread and peace-that he shall know justice and righteousness, freedom and security, an equal opportunity and an equal chance to do his best, not only in our own lands, but throughout the world. And in that faith let us march toward the clean world our hands can make.
Those words have real meaning at this time when our nation is under so much stress.

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
In proceeding to the meat of my address I would ask this question: What did the Speech from the Throne and the Prime Minister's message contain relating to the matters before the nation so far as this House is concerned? The two speeches reminded me of a university graduate delivering at the request of the faculty a valediction. You know, a valediction is given when a graduate is bidding farewell to the students. The Prime Minister has placed himself in that position. If I might paraphrase, this is what the Prime Minister said: I as Prime Minister have failed you; my government has failed, the just society I promised you was a fake, a fraud; the just society is a far away ideal, a new heaven. I could not help but think that the Leader of the New Democratic Party touched on something very important at that time. To paraphrase the Prime Minister again he said that it is a far away ideal, a new heaven but that he has lost faith. He said in effect that there is no heaven, injustice is everywhere, he cannot do anything about it and that we are all going to-I cannot mention the place opposite heaven. That is what he said.
The two speeches were made up of mere magical phrases. In a nutshell, the Prime Minister's speech that was read can be classified as gobbledygook. The playboy and world traveller has a sense of his own writing, and indeed reading, and a personal affection for beautiful words because he bewailed the mammoth string of wooden cliches which he has used so often to preach his propaganda and dogma about what his ideal is. The two speeches will long be remembered for their hollowness in respect of any positive suggestions to curb the ever-spiralling cost of living which is affecting Canadians at all levels and in respect of a remedy to work out any reasonable solution to the problem of disputes between labour and management.
If I might digress at this point I would say that the western farmer is in trouble today because the government failed to measure up to its responsibilities in the dispute between labour and management and this has made it difficult for grain to be moved to the ports and markets. I would suggest this involves other things such as the postal strike and so on. Then there is the problem of social need in respect of housing, the crying need to solve air, water and noise pollution as well as the need for programs to guarantee job security and retraining and, above all, the need to re-establish respect for law and order.
It seems to me that the Trudeau government, which Canadians in 1968 fondly hoped would carve out and create a just society for all Canadians, has reduced this nation to a mere second-rate power among the smaller nations of the world, and has stripped us of our domestic prosperity, unity and dignity. It has successfully eroded our international respect abroad, responsibility and, indeed, our image. However, in 1972 when the election rolls around this all-powerful, absolute, cruel and heartless government will be defeated at the polls. Senator Cameron may have put his finger on the situation. He is a Liberal senator in the other place. He said recently that if an election were held in Canada at the present time not one federal Liberal would be elected west of the Great Lakes. I think that if he took a look at the situation he would say the same thing in respect of Liberals even east of the Great Lakes. The people are fed up with this government.
This government has neglected the cities. I could carry on in this vein. The two speeches, however, rang out with hollowness. They lacked any content. They were both rhetorical incantations. The verse of the government contains only words and not deeds.
Let us for a moment review the platitudes and the cliches in the Prime Minister's speech, let alone in the Speech from the Throne, in which he attacked us and our leader. The Prime Minister started off in his usual gracious manner. He said he had a hunch that the leaders of all parties, particularly the Official Opposition, would be critical of the Speech from the Throne. Why? Because he must have known before the speech was delivered that it was a weak effort, strong in language but weak in deeds. This is really the kind of government we have today. No one needs to exercise his political capacity or sagacity to reach that conclusion.
What did the Prime Minister say about foreign ownership of Canadian industries which is an important problem today? He attacked the position taken by our leader and the leader of the New Democratic Party. This is a typical statement by the Prime Minister. Perhaps I might paraphrase what he said: We on this side have said, through the offices of a minister reporting to cabinet, that we are in the process of trying to enunciate government policy in this important area in order to avoid a pragmatic or ad hoc approach, but we knew we did not have the support of the opposition on this.
During the election the Prime Minister preached strong nationalism and the taking over by Canada of foreign investments. The moment an election is over there is one thing we can always rely on a Liberal Prime Minister doing. When the election is over, what do they do? They rush to the United States, cap in hand, to get another big, fat loan, as the government of Quebec did and as this government will do. Not only does that aggravate our problems but it mortgages the future of Canadian generations yet unborn through foreign investments and increases Canada's national debt. That is kind of inconsistent. The Prime Minister talks about inconsistencies, yet he preaches one thing on the hustings and does another.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
Of course, one need not go far to find the answer for this. One only needs to read what was printed in Le Devoir in February, 1963. There the Prime Minister wrote about liberal philosophy. I have quoted these words before, and it is time to repeat them, because they place many things in their proper perspective. The article is headed, "Pearson, or the Abdication of the Spirit, by Pierre Elliott-Trudeau". At page 14 of the article the following appears, "Thus, the political philosophy of the Liberal party is simplicity itself." That is what he said, and it is easy to understand. He goes on to say, "Say anything, think anything you like. But put us in power, because we are best fitted to govern."
When he stepped into the leadership of the Liberal party he talked of a just society. But that was merely a

October 13, 1970

vague promise of something to come in the future, if we ever get there. That was merely stalling, because nothing is being done.
Let me go to another subject. What does the Prime Minister say about youth? He said that Canada is a young country. Those are beautiful words. He also said that it is in the youth of our country that we seek our future. Well, any Prime Minister could have said that. We all agree with those words. Then he went on to say:
To the youth the past is of relatively little consequence: their lives are still to be lived.
A poet once wrote that "a land without ruins is a land without memories." Our lack of ruins is in some ways a tribute to our ability in the past to adapt to change.
There is one truism about this statement: the Prime Minister has left the country in ruins. What has the government done for the youth of this country or for youth in general-that is what I ask-except mimic their ways and dress? That is something any man of 50 can accomplish. But that is not what our youth are looking for.
I have asked questions oh this subject. The two ministers, the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), have failed to reform our laws that affect our youth. I have brought before this House several times a bill to amend the Criminal Code, because the code says that any person of seven or over who is competent to know the nature and consequences of a criminal act may be convicted of a crime. The government has managed to build an unenviable record. Not since confederation have such claims been made for a just society and administration of justice. We have incarcerated, during the period this government has been in office, more young men and women in our country that at any time since confederation. Is this a record to be proud of? Is this what the government is doing to youth? Actually, this government is good at bringing about highs-high unemployment, high interest rates, high rates of incarceration and high murder rates. The murder rate in Canada has gone up by 55 per cent. This is the government's record and, while intelligent men and women are placed out of sight and out of mind in penitentiaries, the drug problem continues to grow.
The research centres and the rehabilitation centres recommended by the LeDain Commission have been and are still being ignored. They ought to be set up immediately. In liaison with the provinces, the government ought to run such centres. Their purpose is good, for they would explode the drug fictions and make sure that youth becomes more knowledgeable about the use or misuse of non-medical drugs. Words are not enough. Let us have some deeds.
It is two years since this government took office and since the members of the Privy Council, took up their jobs as the executives of Canada. And what does the government say about all these matters? In its own defence the government blames the courts; and the courts, in their own defence-actually the courts have no method of speaking effectively-say that Parliament made the law. Parliament has tried to get these well spoken script readers to change the law, but we have only had more scripts. Again, we have had words but not
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
deeds. Let me repeat: the government blames the courts and the courts blame Parliament. They say that Parliament passes the laws, and that they must be enforced. What is the government? It is really a sort of classical university unto itself. That is what it is.
This past summer I saw some of the realities of our country. As I drove from Ottawa to Calgary on that great No. 1 trans-Canada highway, I saw young people hitchhiking. This summer more young people in Canada roamed and hitchhiked across the country than ever before. Never before have we seen young men and women hitchhiking across this country as we did this past summer. What were they looking for?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes. They were looking for work and opportunity, and they found no work and no opportunity. They were made promises, but few were kept. On this side of the House we begged the government for a positive program to help them. We begged the government to help those graduating from high schools or universities to find employment and opportunity. Few got work. The government did little. Moreover, it destroyed the morale of our armed forces and even destroyed the militia. Then it tried to establish a playboy army by paying youth to play at soldiering while at the same time we put in mothballs $285 million worth of CF-5 aircraft. Again, there were words but no action.

speechtext: Just look at the Prime Minister's staff.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes. Just look at the staff. There is no policy or plan to assist our youth to get an education or to obtain job retraining. While the Prime Minister permits the dissipation of our best resource, youth, unemployment grows and grows among young people. We hold a record in this regard and then he says, "Canada stands as one of the most happy and enviable facts of the times." I do not think he can take credit for all that has happened in this country since confederation. He went on to say:
Because of all this, our country can be looked upon as a global environment, as an environment exceptionally favourable to the fullness of human development.
When young people leave high school and university and cannot find jobs and when young people cannot enter university because of lack of money, are we allowing them to develop? Let me ask the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang), when they are on the list of the unemployed, are they developing? So I say to the government that this is a time for decision and not a time for rhetorical phrases and procrastination. It is a time for an energizing performance. It is not a time for vacillation. We are living in important times. It is time to restore law and order. It is time to maintain our principles and bring about justice and liberty in the true sense of the word. It is not a time for tergiversation. Above all, it is a time for straight talk and not for political verbi-cide and waffling. The Prime Minister has said:
Some are unable to maintain such a standard because of a lack of education or an absence of the skills necessary in today's world; others are unable to stretch their fixed incomes to meet the increased costs of necessities; still others are temporarily without employment through no fault of their own.
62

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
Let me ask tour questions. What aggravated and accelerated the high cost of living? The government's policies did. Who brought in nineteenth century economic methods to cure inflation? The Prime Minister did. Who aggravated unemployment and dumped people out of work on the unemployment market? The Prime Minister did. Who placed the burden on the underprivileged and on those living below the poverty line in Canada? The Liberal government did.
[DOT] (12.30 p.m.)
The Prime Minister says justice will be obtained when the needs of everyone are satisfied. What have you when most things have been ignored, have deteriorated and all are dissatisfied? The Prime Minister stated in his speech in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, as recorded at page 34 of Hansard:
There is justice when everyone's essential needs are satisfied. This implies a reasonable access for all to the goods owned and produced by the country. Now, work is the normal mode of access to the goods on which life depends; it therefore cannot be disassociated from the right to live.
Has the high cost of living brought justice to the old age pensioners or the veterans? Never have they been in such a cost squeeze. Who has been satisfied by throwing people out of work and reducing the low income pensioners and others to destitution? Nobody. Is that the just society?
My charge against this government is that economic justice is rationed. When justice is rationed, how can the ideal of the just society be even a vision let alone a realization? The Prime Minister promised a heaven. He has lost his faith. Now we are left to believe in that other place where all people are suffering.
What about his brave words regarding pollution? The Prime Minister has talked about the ability to set up a number of laws to deal with pollution. For two years I have been raising a question in this House. I use this only as an example. Each year one and a half million visit Banff national park. Raw sewage from the government administrative offices and the government's facilities which they supply during the months of June, July, August and September is being poured into the beautiful, colourful and clean Bow River which crosses Alberta and joins up with the Saskatchewan River and eventually flows into Lake Winnipeg. This is because the government is expropriating practically all free enterprise except the big corporations. Imperial Oil and Canadian Pacific Railway can move in, but the little man is out. While the government talks about doing something concerning pollution, they are not even cleaning up their own household. It is a speech of words and no deeds.
The situation is so bad on the Bow River that 60 miles upstream cattle have died from the pollution caused by this government that talks about fighting the pollution of air, water and noise. The government has now set up a committee. That will mean another delay. I hope my expression will be parliamentary when I say that when I listen to their story about pollution I think, what bloody rot!
What about the cities? The Prime Minister blames the housing crisis on the framework of the Canadian constitution. He says that according to the constitution we cannot rush into the situation like a bull in a china shop. He seems to be out of date. The late Bob Winters started a mammoth housing project after World War II. That was the beginning of a national housing scheme which built houses across this nation and which started suburbia. In a period of 18 months the D.efenbaker government poured $700 million into housing. This was in 1957 and 1958. This would be a lot more today if we compare the present proportion of our budget. While we now have a $13 billion budget, in those days the budget was only $5 billion or $6 billion. If the late Robert Winters was able to do so much when he was the cabinet minister in charge of housing, why cannot the Prime Minister do the same as we move into the seventies?
What we need is a housing program that will rock this nation, one that will work for the average man. Unless a person earns $8,000 to $12,000 he cannot purchase a house in the Montreal, Winnipeg, Calgary or Vancouver areas. This is for the rich. There is nothing for the poor. That is the just society. Is that the far-away ideal we heard about during the election campaign?

The late Premier Johnson of Quebec saw infiltrating revolutionary forces in his province. He saw revolutionary forces and crime syndicates in Montreal, Winnipeg, Calgary, Vancouver and Toronto. He asked the federal government to please set up a royal commission to tabulate how those people were working, the countries from which they were infiltrating and who they were working with. Had this been done we would today have the evidence to lay before the administrative and police officers as well as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. We would be able to handle the FLQ problem. While we asked for that action for two long years the government said, "Oh, we don't need it". We wonder how close they are to this situation when they refuse to find out the facts and the evidence.
The Prime Minister will not yield to the request of the opposition to investigate syndicated crime in our urban centres. All words, no action! Appeasement has never promoted lasting peace. Understanding the problem will achieve a solution, if we act.
The greatest injustice done by this government to any class of people outside of the average men in the urban centres is the injustice that has been done to the treaty Indians. Nothing is more important to a treaty Indian than his treaties. This is the cry of his generation. Here lies the cultural gap between the now white generation and the now red generation, and I am talking about the colour in a colloquial sense and not in a philosophical sense.

October 13, 1970

Before the Indian Act is repealed, before the dictatorial, bureaucratic, unsympathetic white paper is implemented, the treaty rights concerning the Indians' land, culture, way of life and inalienable rights, as guaranteed, must be defined, clarified and judicially defined. Therefore this government, as was promised by the Pearson government and died on the order paper when we were defeated as a government, should immediately set up an Indian commission and administrative board with all the necessary informalities so that evidence judicially admissible or inadmissible should be made admissible before this board in order that this board can ascertain the treaty rights of those Indians and so that the proper facts and documentation which are presently denied by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development can be ascertained. This board must be armed with the proper powers to subpoena witnesses, hear evidence and force the production of documentation which is being denied the Indians. The most skilful lawyers and advisers should be placed at the disposal of the Indians.
When members on this side of the House make the positive suggestion that the government hire and pay these people to ascertain those rights, the government says it is not necessary. For ten years a case has been pending in the Exchequer Court involving the Blackfoot reservation Indians who are asking for the establishment of their treaty rights. They are also asking for compensation for land abuse and expropriation. For ten long years that case has laid idle. This is not because the court will not hear the case but because the Indians do not have a lawyer. One lawyer undertook to act in connection with the petition. Then he wrote to the Department of Indian Affairs asking whether he could receive at least his expenses. But he got no answer, no co-operation. Is this the just soc'ety? It is just in words, but not in deeds. Until we have achieved this promise of legal assistance, this nat'on can never achieve the destiny visualized and expected by our forefathers, nor can we as Canadians point a finger at other nations, whether they be the United States of America or the countries in Africa, as to their rationing of justice.

I have only a few more remarks to make. I shall not abuse the courtesy of the House. But I will say this. The constitution has guaranteed the Indians their rights, if rights they are-I could elaborate on this theme if I had time. Those rights arose because of treaties made in the name of the Crown. The terms of the constitution placed the Indians under federal jurisdiction. An attempt is now being made to assign this responsibility to the provinces as part of an effort by the govern-
The Address-Mr. Pringle
ment to evade its full responsibility. It is being done in the name of justice and, we are told, following consultation. What really happened? They hired a few Indians on the breadline to go out and try to sell this program.
But let me ask these questions. What Indian has asked for land ownership which would result in provincial taxation of Indian reservations? What Indian has asked that the Canadian constitution be changed to remove any reference to Indians or Indian lands? What Indian has asked that treaties be brought to an end? What group of Indians has asked the government to exclude from its special consideration half of the Indian population in Canada? Mr. Speaker, these questions are self-answered. No Indians have asked for these things. Yet this policy is being rammed down their throats.
The just society is a far-away ideal. The Indian had faith, and what he was promised was a heaven. It proved to be a fraud and a fake. The heaven has turned into hell for these people, who are now demanding action.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am indeed happy to associate myself with those who have extended compliments to the hon. member from Bourassa (Mr. Trudel) who so ably moved the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I also congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for selecting a member of this stalwart group on the immediate left of the Speaker who are entrusted with the balance of power in this chamber and who are affectionately referred to by the opposition as the government rump. I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I failed also to extend sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault) on the occasion of his elevation to the position of Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour. As unofficial leader of the rump in Canada's twenty-eighth Parliament, he discharged his duties faithfully and well. Our loss, here in the rump, can only be compared in depth to the expressions of sadness and grief exhibited by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis) as a result of the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour being reseated in another section of the chamber.
My compliments also go to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) who seconded the reply. I congratulate him on the context of his remarks which brought a message to the chamber from Canadian agriculture. His long association with various segments of our agricultural industry, as a practising farmer, is invaluable to Parliament in general and to the Standing Committee on Agriculture in particular.
Notwithstanding the apparent determination of the Official Opposition to obstruct progress or permit change in needed farm legislation, farmer producers have been striving to throw off the yoke of the status quo and accept authority, provided by provincial enabling legislation, for production planning coupled with the responsibility of marketing. This is especially true of commodity groups which are heavily dependent on domestic sales.
Failure to complete the report stage and third reading of Bill C-196, the Canada Grain Act, as amended by the Standing Committee on Agriculture, may serve the inter-
64

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Pringle
ests of the grain trade but will provide little or no solace to grain farmers now desperately in need of the provisions in the Act to improve and expedite the marketing of grain according to world customer demand. The hope of our grain farmers, and indeed of all producer-oriented Members of Parliament from all parties, is that the Official Opposition will agree to permit the debate on Bill C-196 to proceed in its present status during this new session so that the bill can be passed without further unnecessary delay.
The second farm bill to fall prey to the sabotage tactics of the Official Opposition was Bill C-197, an Act to establish a farm products marketing council and to authorize the establishment of national marketing agencies for farm products.
Mr. Speaker, although I have been associated with Canadian agri-business for many years, no one has satisfactorily explained to me why farmer producers have been denied the right to place a price on their products. The purchaser quoted the price and the farmer took what he was offered. With the exception of the Wheat Board and the Dairy Commission, little or no federal ground rules, known as enabling legislation, have been enacted to allow commodity groups in competition with other commodity groups to discipline themselves and establish a reasonable degree of stability. On the contrary, farmer producers have actually been encouraged to produce in heavy surplus, to build unmanageable inventories, resulting in disastrous market prices which on a regular basis dropped below the cost of efficient production. This system has enabled secondary industry to farm the farmers while the Canadian taxpayers picked up the tab in the form of subsidies just prior to the collapse of a commodity group into bankruptcy.
Consumers have also unwittingly been the innocent victims of this system. Heavy surpluses forced prices to farmers down, although secondary industry usually managed to maintain satisfactory margins. The consumers jumped with joy, only to find that within a period of time farmers were forced into alternative production, creating shortages which shoved prices to a high level, more than wiping out any advantages gained during the low-price period. Farmer producers, with unpaid feed bills in areas of specialized production, either lost their farms or, in attempting to switch to other commodities, went further into debt to provide additional capital.
Therefore, under the old system of surplus and shortage consumers have suffered with producers. The solution has proven to be production and marketing stability. By this I mean ample high quality production with manageable inventories, providing an adequate service to processing and distribution outlets at stable prices and in competition with other food items. This system may curtail the profits of some segments of secondary industry. However, producer confidence, inspired by stability, encourages farmers to take advantage of technological progress by investing in mechanical aids which improve efficiency and lower costs.
A moment ago I suggested that the solution has proven to be production and marketing stability. I use the past tense because existing marketing boards operating within the scope of provincial enabling legislation have already
brought during the last nine years a degree of stability to their commodity groups virtually unheard of in the history of Canadian agriculture.
I say this while acknowledging the fact that a threat to interprovincial movement of poultry products now exists in Canada. It has been dubbed the "chicken and egg war". Those of us who are familiar with the sequence of events know that each step taken by provincial governments in order to maintain stability was the direct result of actions taken by commodity groups who have refused to adopt the concept of orderly production coupled with orderly marketing through marketing boards.
It is no secret that Quebec egg producers pleaded with producers in other poultry surplus provinces to adopt a system of supply management and orderly marketing which would assure some price stability in Quebec. This took place over a period of years. They wanted some stability that was comparable to other commodities in other provinces which were operating through producer marketing boards. When the Quebec egg producers' pleas were ignored the Quebec agency, I would say somewhat in desperation, placed interprovincial movement of eggs into Quebec under the jurisdiction of the Quebec board. They did not eliminate interprovincial movement of eggs into Quebec, and I place emphasis on that fact.
During this period certain promoters known in the poultry trade as integrators apparently decided to invest heavily in facilities for broiler production in Quebec. We now come to the chicken part of the "chicken and egg war". It is interesting to note that while broiler marketing boards were operating successfully in other provinces, Quebec producers were either unable or unwilling-I am more inclined to believe the former to be true-to establish a broiler marketing board in Quebec. Quebec producers with little or no capital were persuaded to provide land and labour at prices considered unrealistic in all other parts of Canada. It was not long before huge unwieldy surpluses of broilers began to build up in Quebec and subsequently went into interprovincial movement to all sections of Canada at what must be considered distress prices by all people knowledgeable in the broiler industry.
It is inconceivable to believe that the promoter integrators of Quebec who enjoyed mark-up revenues from feed sales, egg hatching and processing would expect farmer producers in other parts of Canada to go bankrupt and abandon their investment. It is also paradoxical that Quebec egg producers showed the way to the other provinces. It was they who paved the way for resumption of stability, something in which all farmers across the land are interested, which has been lacking in agriculture through the years but which is now finally finding its way to the surface. All other provinces, with the possible exception of Newfoundland, have with the co-operation of provincial enabling legislation issued orders relating to interprovincial movement of broilers similar to the Quebec order regarding the interprovincial movement of eggs.
This unilateral action on the part of provincial marketing boards and governments was taken as a last resort and not without considerable apprehension as to the future of interprovincial trade in Canada. Let it be a

October 13, 197 0

matter of record that the broiler commodity groups in all provinces of Canada endeavoured to persuade the promoters in Quebec to cut back their production and to work out a market sharing system so it would not be necessary to ask them to hold back their shipments. This is something that had to happen. I have been in touch with most broiler marketing boards in the western provinces, and it is my understanding that some stability is already returning to the market. I have been told there is a shortage of broilers in Ontario but on checking I find that a bothersome surplus still exists. Broiler chicken is still the cheapest meat on the counter and will continue to be in the foreseeable future. May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was obliged to call it one o'clock, and for the benefit of those who have tuned in late, I may say that I was discussing the sequence relating to what is now known in the vernacular as the "chicken and egg wars", I was referring to the problems relating to interprovincial trade between the various provinces.
Let me make it very clear that I know of no one who holds the Quebec farmer-producer, and I stress that phrase, in his role as a type of hired man, grower accountable for the present dilemma. It is most unfortunate that they undoubtedly are suffering now financially
The Address-Mr. Pringle
as a result this ruthless overproduction. It must be noted that broiler growers everywhere are deeply concerned, but I believe that farmer-producers will find the solution if we grant them the opportunity to do so.
It was suggested on several occasions earlier today that we should support the government of Manitoba which has elected to seek a ruling from the Supreme Court of Canada. I am at a loss to understand how this will solve the problem of interprovincial trade. This may assist Manitoba in shipping eggs into Quebec, if they are successful, but as I previously stated, the Quebec order does not eliminate the interprovincial movement of eggs into the province of Quebec. Other provinces have made similar orders and I should like, if I may, to quote from the last paragraph of the order published by the province of British Columbia. It reads:
Nothing in this order shall prevent any person from bringing into, packing and storing in the Province of British Columbia any import product or from exporting any import product to any place outside the Province.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
But the Province has the jurisdiction to regulate sales, and is doing this to the best of its ability. In fact, Quebec is granting contracts and orders for the inter-provincial movement of eggs at present. But let us suppose that the steps taken by the Manitoba government are successful. It will mean that the efforts of one province in Canada to regulate interprovincial trade have been ruled ultra vires. However, the other orders made by at least eight other provinces are not exactly the same as the Quebec order. That means we would have to go back to the Supreme Court of Canada-I am not a lawyer but I am advised that this would have to happen-on each different order, and I am not too sure whether my tenure of office would be long enough for me to see the end result. But I know what it would be if we could provide the producer-growers of Canada with a marketing act which would be operated by producers and be satisfactory to them.
I think we all agree that trade restrictions at provincial borders under individual provincial jurisdiction are going to be a stop gap measure at best. A national producer marketing act operated by producers, designed to challenge the various commodity groups to compete with each other for their fair share of the consumers' dollar would provide the best vehicle. I therefore renew my plea to hon. members opposite to permit the enactment of such legislation as soon as possible.
Canadian farmer-producers, through their various commodity group organizations, are ready, willing and able to shoulder the responsibility of stable food production. They possess the expertise and desire to manage their own affairs.
I was more than pleased with the emphasis on pollution control included in the Speech from the Throne. Since my constituency is located in the beautiful Fraser Valley, the acknowledged garden spot of the world, any type of pollution quickly becomes a matter of deep concern. This is evidenced by the formation of a number of groups willingly giving of their time and effort to fight pollution of all kinds wherever it becomes apparent. Perhaps one of the most active groups is known as SPEC,

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Thompson
which stands for the Society for Pollution and Ecological Control. This group is not only dedicated to attacking industrial waste, whether air, land or water, but is also concentrating on the control of pollution at the home owner level. In this particular, area we are concerned with fighting pollution more than with fighting industry. We do not believe that the elimination of industry will cure pollution, but we believe that we have the technological knowledge at present to cure pollution and to permit industry to continue to operate.
These groups have recognized that the use of detergents in automatic washing machines, overuse of pesticides, incinerator burning, and in fact outdoor barbecuing, all add to pollution. It is interesting to note today that a member of the society in my home town of Chil-liwac, Mr. John Rogers, has been petitioning for a survival day for all Canada for many months. I am sure he would be gladdened by the knowledge that the nation's capital is attempting the experiment on October 14, and I wish it well even though I am not too good at riding my son's bicycle.
Another problem of deep concern relating to the ecological future in my area is the proposed flooding of the Skagit Valley by the department of lighting of the city of Seattle. Although the existing dam is located in the United States, the flooding will take place in Canada. This would create a ten mile addition to Ross Lake with a gradient of only 100 feet or less so that only a very small draw down would create a large area of mud flats. It is my understanding that the International Rivers Improvement Act, passed Parliament on July 11, 1955, requires federal permits approving the altering of any waterway crossing an international border. We are, therefore, hopeful that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) will take whatever measures are necessary to persuade the Seattle department of lighting to seek additional power elsewhere.
In closing may I say to all hon. members within the sound of my voice that the 100th birthday of British Columbia's entrance into confederation takes place in 1971. Plans are now being developed throughout the province for a year of meaningful celebration, and worthwhile projects are being projected commemorating the past 100 years whilst steadfastly looking to the future.
May I at this time properly thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), his cabinet and the government for the very generous gift of $10 million to the people of B.C. from the people of all Canada to assist in paying the cost. Many fine and worthwhile buildings will be made available to the people of B.C. which would have undoubtedly been denied to them without the generous gift of this government. I therefore, extend a warm and sincere invitation to everyone: come to British Columbia and join with us in 1971. You will receive a welcome unsurpassed anywhere in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to take part in the Throne Speech debate. I wish to offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Trudel) and seconder (Mr. Douglas (Assiniboia)) of the motion which brought the Throne Speech before us in the House of Commons. It is an honour to be so selected.
I find the Throne Speech to be a very interesting document. It contains many platitudinous statements with which practically anybody of any loyalty to our country cannot but agree, yet many of these are hollow in that the meanings of the words are neither interpreted for us, nor are the statements which follow the embodiment of what is meant. In fact, many of them are contradictory.
Today I want to draw the attention of the House to one aspect of the remarks made in the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne states that the passing of the 60's and the beginning of the 70's reminds us that Canada faces a new age, an age which will be subject to forces not all of which are yet comprehended or understood, forces which will proceed from external as well as internal origin. I agree with that statement. I only wish that some of the happenings and events that are taking place today might indicate that the government as well agreed with it.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
It is a new age not so much because of changed circumstances, but new because of changed values and attitudes.
I think that is a fair statement too, Mr. Speaker, but what disturbs me is that there is no attempt in this Speech from the Throne to define or explain what these changed values or attitudes are. Like a lot of other Canadians today, I am concerned about what they might be. The next paragraph of the speech is as follows:
Because of the clash between these new values and the old, because of the quest by the young and the disillusioned for some resolution of attitudes, we live in a period of tenseness and unease. It is an age frequented by violence as desperate men seek ill-defined goals; an age of frustration as gentle men question impatiently old assumptions.
I question many of the old assumptions that are before us, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to hear the government state more clearly what some of these new attitudes and changed values are, because therein does my concern lie. Thus, Mr. Speaker, my remarks are going to be based upon these statements which I have quoted from the Speech from the Throne.
I believe that this is an historic but sad day for Canada. The government of our great land, while being intimidated on the one hand by the FLQ, which it knows as well as we do is a revolutionary movement in sympathy with and in full support of the communist movements of Cuba, Algeria and elsewhere, has chosen today to announce its recognition of the communist government of China. Political leaders in Algiers, Peking and Moscow must be very smug and happy today. Likewise it must be a dark, discouraging and frustrating experience for our friends who directly confront communist China, such as Korea, Viet Nam, Thailand and many other countries which by their own experience know the ruthless strategy of communism, and whose citizens have struggled and died for the hope of freedom. I think of the Phillipines and of Hungary. I think of Indonesia, of Czechoslovakia, and of at least another score of nations across the world. Is this where the changing values and new attitudes are?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) said earlier today that Canada has no statement to make one way or another in regard to the claim of the Peking

October 13, 1970

communist government that Taiwan is an inalienable, territorial part of China. Who does the minister think he is kidding? Do we throw 14 million people into the hands of the communists without even a quiver of conscience? How could any government of a free nation, or any conscientious liberty-loving person be neutral between freedom and slavery?
A few days ago the death was announced of M. Dala-dier, once leader of pre-war France. I cannot help but wonder if we are in the midst of another Munich betrayal.
In 1936 in the Council Chamber of the old League of Nations in Geneva, the Emperor of Ethiopia, under whom it was my privilege to serve directly for some eight years, when the pressure of events had caused him to realize that passiveness of the League had neutralized any action for justice in face of the invading fascist armies in his country, said, "God and history will not forget." Perhaps God and history will not forget today either.
But, Mr. Speaker, referring again to the changing values and new attitudes which the Speech from the Throne spoke about, I must say that as a Member of Parliament and as a citizen of Canada I am disturbed and saddened by the events of the past nine days. A tragedy of numbing severity and of frightening ramifications at two distinct levels has stunned the country. On one level we have witnessed the spectacle of warped and desperate men playing at the same time magistrate and executioner in mad pursuit of their goals. For the safety of two innocent lives we have but two responses-hope and prayer. For two equally innocent families, one cannot verbalize or articulate sympathy equal to what all Canadians feel.
At a collective level as a nation we have witnessed a tragedy no less inestimable. For the past nine days we have seen the subjugation of democratic values to terrorism, the subjugation of human life to political expediency, the subjugation of justice by law to oppression by anarchy. We allow this situation to continue only at our individual and collective peril. Frightened Canadians in Quebec and in every other province, I believe, look bewilderingly for leadership.
I am reminded, Mr. Speaker, that just about three years ago-in fact it was on October 17, 1967-I raised a question in this House regarding reports that appeared in the press, which had appeared throughout the summer and during the following months, concerning guerilla terrorist training activity taking place in the Laurentians. I talked about the huge staff at the Cuban pavilion at Expo actually participating in such terrorist training. I talked about the distribution of communist newspapers, and in particular of GRANMA, the official Cuban communist party newspaper which was being distributed freely from the Cuban Expo pavilion.
I was laughed at then, Mr. Speaker, and I found it necessary to write an open letter to the minister of external affairs, the Hon. Paul Martin. I tried to talk to him about the matter, but I could not get anywhere with him with regard to it. So, my open letter was an attempt to bring these things to his attention.
The Address-Mr. Thompson
In this connection, I quote from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Telegram on July 31, 1961, as follows:
Recently there have been overtones of association between small extremist French Canadian separatist groups and alleged guerilla veterans among the bloated staff of the Cuban Expo pavilion. In 1965, half a dozen French Canadian separatists attended "summer courses" at the University of Havana...
The editorial continues:
Cuba, unlike almost all her communist fellow states, is openly playing the oldest communist game of all, violent international revolution.
At that time we did not realize really what was taking place, and we are only now coming to the reality of it.
The federal government is naive to assume that it is dealing with political separatists or with those whose commitment is to change by political means. In that regard I must say that the statement made the other night by Rene Levesque was a commendable one. I am very pleased he made it because he disassociated himself and his organization, which is seeking to bring about change in Canada through legitimate political means, from those who would bring change about through revolution and terrorism.
The abductors of Mr. Cross and Mr. Laporte are members of the FLQ who are committed first and foremost to the destruction of a political system by revolution. These are not the new ideas and attitudes that we want in Canada. These people seize any issue to advance their cause, through violence if necessary. The FLQ is not a political action group working to reform the country. They are revolutionaries. Ascribing middle class values of fair play to these men is not to face up to reality. There can be no middle ground with these desperadoes.
I call upon the government, supported by Parliament, to re-assert that the rule of law, the sanctity of the judicial process shall prevail in this emergency. To bargain with those who would equate reason and reform with abduction and murder is to bargain with no less than the stability of society itself. Any concession to those to whom violence is a political expedient, no matter how small, can only be construed as a sign of insipient weakness and a lack of resolve and commitment to those principles upon which civilized society inevitably rests. To suppose that criminals, who would countenance the taking of innocent lives for their own twisted purposes, will be amicable to reasoned compromise is to ignore historical experience and present realities. I must commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for his statement during the question period today when he resented the fact that certain members and elements of the press continue to call these men political prisoners-those whose release is being sought. They are what he said- criminals and brigands, and I think we should deal with them.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
It disturbs me to hear men on television and radio, who would pretend to lead public opinion, say they cannot make a moral judgment on these issues until they know more of the facts. The country is responsible. Just as we members of this chamber extend the responsibility to

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Thompson others, we carry public responsibility as well. The agony of decision must not obscure the issues involved. The choice is between a society of order and justice, where the majority determines the destiny of a nation, or a predatory state of anarchism where a nasty, brutish and short life is expendable to the dictates of a minority. Concession in this context can lead only to further concession, as we have already witnessed. The rule of law in a free society is non-negotiable.
Realizing as I do the gravity of the situation, and conscious as I am of the responsibility of all members of the House of Commons to assure the Canadian people that we shall never succumb to lawless terrorism, I call upon the government to implement without delay the following five-point program. I call upon the Prime Minister to make a nation-wide address to the Canadian people to reassert the primary rule of law in this country and to assure them of the government's resolve to take measures of appropriate severity to the gravity of the situation. Acting upon the authority conferred upon it by Section 91 subsection (1) of the British North America Act, I call upon the government to declare that the political kidnappings in the city of Montreal are matters affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada and henceforth will be treated as a federal responsibility, working in close co-operation with the provincial and municipal authorities. We have already seen a partial step in this regard, although even that was bungled this morning. When we see troops in battle dress in the House of Commons or even on the Hill, we admit our own weakness or ability to judge the situation. It is good that this situation has been corrected.
Third, I call upon the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) to announce a substantial award, plus executive clemency, to anyone who can provide authoritative information leading to the apprehension of the criminals responsible for these two abductions. Many times in the past this has proven to be a very useful strategy. Fourth, I call upon the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet to commit such officers of the RCMP and of the Canadian armed forces as are necessary to ensure the speedy apprehension of those responsible for these heinous crimes. I invite the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, and the provincial and municipal authorities, to explore in detail the feasibility of commencing an immediate house to house search of any area where reasonable suspicion exists that FLQ cells are operative. It is a travesty of justice that persons are able to hold the men whom they have abducted without the forces of the law being able to apprehend them or even know where they are.
As a member of the House of Commons, I hereby serve notice that at the earliest opportunity I shall attempt to secure an amendment to subsection (1) of section 233 of the Criminal Code of Canada concerning the crime of kidnapping to make kidnapping for political ends a capital offence subject to the death penalty.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

As the law stands now our hands are tied.
This is a concrete program born not of panic but of resolve, put forward not in turbid confusion but in the unshakable conviction that whatever be the problems of our society they are not solvable by vigilante lawlessness. It is a program which would not only unite the Canadian people in their determination to continue a society which effects change by non-violent democratic processes but would also serve notice upon those who would use terrorist tactics to erode the confidence of the people and to eradicate a nation's values that such methods will not and cannot succeed. To forfeit this opportunity to clearly express our values and the depth of our commitment to those values would be an individual and collective abdication of our responsibilities.
In closing, I should like to refer to another statement contained a little further along in the Speech from the Throne. I would challenge the Prime Minister to act upon these words which basically are his. These are the words:
... there is more need than ever before to preserve as constant values truth, honesty, excellence and relevance; that a society which is not inspired by love and compassion is not worthy of the name.
I would add to that statement "that is not inspired by love, compassion and justice is not worthy of that name". Certainly, the people of Canada are expecting more than they are getting from the government of Canada today in this crisis.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Trudel) and the seconder (Mr. Douglas (Assiniboia)) of the Speech from the Throne for the tremendous job they did in this respect. I should like to participate in this debate today to discuss the developments in our economy and in our economic policy that have taken place since I presented my budget to this House in March.
Our perspectives on the economy and on economic policy are changing with changing events. It may be helpful if I begin by recalling to hon. members how we viewed the situation last March, based on the facts then available. The data on the year 1969 was nearly complete. It revealed that the inflation gripping the country had carried prices up at a rate of about 4f per cent. Our fiscal and monetary policies had finally, after some delay, succeeded in reducing the rate of growth of demand after mid-year. This lower growth of demand had induced lower profit rates, but had brought no reduction in the rate of wage rate increases. As for prices, we were able to say at that time that we could see some hopeful signs of a lower rate of price increase, but nothing more. It looked as though the stage was set for some dampening of the inflationary forces, but one could not be sure. The Prices and Incomes Commission had just concluded its agreement with the business community and we were conscious that any success they might achieve on their front would permit more rapid relaxation of the restrictive policies.
In these circumstances, we struck a stance for a moderate expansion in fiscal policy. We planned for a reduced budgetary surplus and for increased non-budgetary expenditures, which taken together implied an increase in our cash outlays from the previous fiscal year of about
[Mr. Pringle.)
October 13, 1970

three-quarters of a billion dollars. In planning our increased expenditures we concentrated on high priority programs such as those of regional economic expansion, housing and manpower training. We also took particular care to ensure that much of the new stimulus would be directed to regions of traditionally higher unemployment.
At the same time, because of the continuing inflationary threat, we took out some insurance by planning for a system of controls over buying by consumers on credit and by extending our measure for deferred depreciation on non-residential construction where we felt the thrust of construction costs was particularly strong and infectious.
In outlining this policy position, I stated clearly that the government would respond quickly to changes in the economic outlook with changes in its policy measures.
On the basis of this policy position, I anticipated that output and employment would move upward in 1970 though at a lower rate than in 1969. I indicated that there would be some increase in unemployment accompanied by difficult labour negotiations and strikes. I also held out the hope that price advances would be somewhat less vigorous. These expectations have so far been borne out by developments, though in somewhat fuller measure.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to review the economic developments to date this year in some detail. The economy has been growing less rapidly this year than last. In the first half of the year the national output, apart from price changes, grew at an annual rate of just under 2\ per cent. This compares with a rate of a little below 4J per cent in the last half of 1969.
Some sectors of the economy have been stronger than others. Growth of the demand for consumer goods and services and for new capital goods have been outpaced by demands of governments and even more by demands for our exports. In the personal sector, a slower growth of income has led to lower growth in the demand for goods and services, especially in the first quarter of this year.
Investment in residential construction, following the lower starts of late 1969 and early 1970, experienced a sharp fall, especially in the second quarter. We are now, however, on the way up. Housing starts, reflecting the March budget's injection of an additional $150 million in CMHC loans, have been rising for several months. In September they were running at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 185,000, up from about 175,000 in July and August and an average 137,000 in the second quarter.
Business spending on new capital has been sluggish so far this year. On non-residential construction spending was no higher in the first half than the average level of last year. This is in spite of an increase of about 15 per cent indicated for this year in the surveys of investment intentions. The intentions surveys also suggested much higher levels of spending by business on machinery and equipment this year, but in the first half this spending was some 6 per cent below 1969. These shortfalls of spending below intentions reflect in part the deliberate choices of business in the face of their expectations of
The Address-Mr. Benson
profits and sales. But they also reflect, especially in regard to construction expenditures, the strikes and lockouts in the construction industry. These disputes have produced an 82-per cent increase in the number of man days lost in the construction industry in the first eight months of this year compared with the same period in 1969. Labour peace in this sector would, I am confident, give rise to a marked renewal of activity.
Let me turn now to two expansive areas of demand this year. I refer first to demands by governments for goods, services and new capital assets. Taking all levels of government together their expenditures have risen by about 8 per cent in the first half of this year as compared with some 5 per cent in the second half of last year. The increase this year has been particularly heavy in the second quarter.
Secondly, exports have been a most dynamic force in the economy this year. After having grown at about 7 per cent over the last half of 1969, they grew by some 9 per cent in the first half of this year, most of this increase being concentrated in the first quarter. The latest figures, for August, show some decline from the very high plateau achieved earlier in the year, but exports continue to run well above the figures for the last quarter of 1969. Our sales to countries other than the United States have been the most buoyant. On a seasonally adjusted basis export sales to the United States were lower in August than in December by 7 per cent, but sales to other countries were higher by 14 per cent.
Merchandise imports have been on a declining trend this year and as a consequence the balance of trade has been very strong indeed. Even when this favorable balance is offset by a first half deficit on non-merchandise transactions of about a billion dollars, the current account of the balance of payments is left in surplus by nearly $300 million.
This strong trade surplus, reflecting in part our better price performance, combined with strong inflows of capital to produce considerable upward pressure on the Canadian dollar. We decided at the end of May that we should not resist this pressure any longer. The alternatives were to revalue or allow the dollar to float. In the event, we decided to cease for the time being to purchase sufficient U.S. dollars to keep the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar in the market from exceeding its par-value of 92i U.S. cents by more than 1 per cent. Since then the exchange rate has been allowed to respond to market forces. I shall refer later to the effects of the subsequent rise in the exchange value of our currency.
I would like now to discuss the labour situation in some detail. The population of the country that is of working age grows at a fairly predictable rate. The rate was about 2.6 per cent last year and we expect it to be about the same this year. What is very much less predictable is the proportion of those in the population of working age who will offer themselves for employment. This proportion, technically referred to as the labour force participation rate, has been showing some wild gyrations lately. These gyrations very seriously affect our unemployment figures. For example at a given level of employment a difference of 1 percentage point in the participation rate-which is the order of magnitude we
70

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Benson
have been lately-can make a difference of If percentage points in the unemployment rate. This is a very serious matter. We believe the factors involved in these swings include the movement of students in and out of the labour force, the impact of the manpower training program and the reactions of potential income earners in a family unit to the fortunes of the principal breadwinner. These factors interact in a complicated way. Predictions and assessments of the unemployment situation are greatly complicated by this situation.
Another factor of considerable importance in assessing the unemployment situation in the country has not received much public attention to date. This is the dramatic acceleration in recent years in the time lost in work stoppages owing to industrial disputes. The figure of man-days lost per quarter from this cause has been rising at an average rate of 25 per cent per year since 1962 and has now become very large. Disputes in some industries cause unemployment in others. In fact, the second quarter seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was probably a half to three quarters of a percentage point higher for this reason. In referring to this matter I do not wish in any way to minimize the distress that unemployment causes. We must, however, recognize that it would be futile to use fiscal and monetary policy to try to eliminate unemployment arising from this cause.
In following the developing situation in respect of unemployment, it is important to keep a close watch on the number of those who have been unemployed more than three months. For these persons the lack of employment is obviously even more serious than for those who are out of work for shorter periods. This proportion is small. In August, people in this category comprised 1.7 per cent of the labour force, and the figure has remained remarkably stable, indicating a high order of resiliency in our economy.
I have spent some time, Mr. Speaker, in commenting on these special features of the labour supply situation because all members of this House share the government's deep concern with the fact that unemployment is as high as it is.

I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that we have been rewarded in our struggle against inflation. I spoke earlier, Mr. Speaker, about the policy measures adopted in my March budget to deal with the economic situation at that time. I have traced the economic developments since then. I would like now to describe in some detail the policy responses of the government and the specific measures we have taken to deal with this changing situation. The government's economic policy objective is to give to the economy the maximum stimulus that can be provided without unleashing another and inevitably more damaging round of inflation.
In pursuing this objective, we are continuously reassessing the degree of stimulus that can be provided within the terms of the objective. In this reassessing we have been greatly encouraged by the more moderate price increases. As the new price information brightened _nto sharper focus, the government felt that it could take a more relaxed fiscal stance. We are still very worried by the continued increase of wage costs. We continue to hope, however, that moderating prices hold some promise that wage demands might soon be scaled down. Given the lags in the impact of policy changes, which we consider carefully in our planning, we felt a progressive

October 13, 1970

adjustment of the stance was warranted. This view developed before we were pressed by events into allowing an appreciation of the dollar to occur. We recognized that this appreciation would put pressure on our exporters and on our import competing industries.
One of our first moves was to drop the insurance policy we had taken out in the form of a projected control over consumer credit.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada has explained in his statement of August 31 that monetary policy since early in the year has sought to relax the very tight credit conditions which prevailed at the beginning of the year. The bank rate has been progressively lowered from 8 per cent to 61 per cent. Market rates of interest, especially for shorter term securities, have fallen this year. The rate on long term government of Canada bonds is down roughly half a percentage point and treasury bill yields are down about 21 percentage points. Since March of this year the average monthly increase in the seasonally adjusted private money supply at annual rates has been 12.1 per cent.
I should like also to refer to the measures I announced at the meeting of Ministers of Finance and Provincial Treasurers at Winnipeg in June. On that occasion I announced that the government of Canada would undertake to accelerate payment to the provinces of tax collections we make on their behalf. This has the effect of increasing our non-budgetary requirements this year-in effect the funds we put into the economy in this way-by $150 million. In addition, I announced that equalization payments to provinces would be increased by $60 million over the $867 million originally planned, on the basis of new data that had become available since the estimates.
Finally, I announced that $150 million remaining to be spent under the technical and vocational training schools program would be disbursed to the provinces in this fiscal year and the next. This, coupled with a further extra $15 million of disbursements to the provinces under other programs, added $90 million more to our budgetary expenditures for this year. Thus the effect of these measures was to add $150 million to our budgetary requirements and $150 million to our non-budgetary requirements or $300 million in all-a very considerable figure.
We have taken further important steps since the June announcements. Let us consider budgetary expenditures first. Equalization payments to the provinces for the current year have been raised by another $50 million to approximately $975 million owing to the impact of yet further new data. Payments under social insurance programs such as the Canada Assistance Plan have risen and will add further to the purchasing power in the private sector. Hon. members will be aware of the important effort and expenditure we made this past summer in connection with student summer employment programs.
