Let me now summarize the progressive expansion which has taken place in the government's fiscal and monetary policies in step with the steady easing of inflationary pressures over the past several months.
In the budget last March, there was a significant easing of fiscal restraint, with the government's cash requirement undergoing a swing of around three-quarters of a billion dollars from the previous year. At the meeting of
Finance Ministers and Provincial Treasurers in Winnipeg last June I indicated that outlays to the provinces would increase by some $300 million to cover accelerated transfers of tax revenue, accelerated payment of technical and vocational training school grants and higher equalization payments. Since that time it has been estimated that equalization payments to the provinces will be further increased this year by $50 million. The student summer employment program launched by the government, together with increased payments under various social insurance programs, will add another $73 million to current expenditures.
An additional $100 million has been allocated in the present calendar year to finance the construction of
15,000	housing units for families with moderate incomes. And today I have announced plans for new expenditure of $60 million of programs aimed directly at relieving unemployment where conditions are most severe.
On the monetary side, there has also been a significant easing of restraint. Since March of this year, the money supply in private hands has increased at a seasonally adjusted annual rate averaging 12.1 per cent. Rates of interest are significantly lower, particularly for shorter-term securities.
Mr. Speaker, this review should assure all members of the House that the government is maintaining an alert, continuous watch for opportunities to move the economy forward. Just as soon as we have felt reasonable confidence that our anti-inflation policies were bringing favourable results we have moved to stimulate the economy. We are anxious and determined to achieve a faster rate of growth and higher employment. But we know we cannot achieve and retain this prize through inflation.
I would like to make a few observations on the outlook as it now appears to us. In the government's view the pace of our advance and the support we can give to it will be determined very largely by developments in the private sector of the economy. A key is the performance of costs. The recovery of capital investment depends very directly upon the outlook for profits. This is turn depends upon productivity and wage costs. The potential demand exists, for there is today no generalized over-capacity in capital equipment and structures such as we have known in certain earlier periods. On the recovery of capital investment depends the recovery of employment and personal incomes and hence consumer spending. We can expect strength from government expenditures and exports, the forces which have sustained the economy this year.
As our economy moves forward our governments and industries will have growing needs for funds. Having in mind the pressure that appreciation puts upon our industries in direct competition with foreign producers, I would urge those who are contemplating borrowing to consider very carefully whether they have fully availed themselves of the competitive services of the Canadian capital market before they decide to float issues outside of Canada.
We anticipate a steady improvement in our employment situation, though the winter ahead will be a difficult one. We shall need a substantial annual rate of real growth before any marked improvement in the unem-
[Mr. Benson.l
October 13, 1970

ployment rate will be forthcoming. These are the hard facts.
We believe that the economy is capable of returning to the rates of growth which will reduce the unemployment rate significantly over the next four or five quarters. We believe that our policy stance will guide the economy on this course. The government will do the people of Canada no service if it rekindles the inflation by seeking to force an advance more rapid than productivity improvement and cost moderation will permit. The government will continue to be alert, as it has been alert, to reassess the developments in costs, in productivity and in prices, which must in the end determine the maximum degree of stimulus that the economy can safely absorb. When we can take further action to spur the economy closer to the goal of full employment and growth with stable prices we shall do so. We believe the stage is now set for the recovery of employment-perhaps slowly at first but at an accelerating pace. A strong growth of employment and the reduction of unemployment consistent with good price performance and moderating costs is the priority goal of our economic policy.

Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne and in the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this debate, this House has witnessed an almost unparalleled barrage of high-flown phrases and wordy platitudes. No doubt the speech writers in the Prime Minister's office and the other draftsmen responsible for these documents, are congratulating themselves on their command of language and esoteric concepts. But what the Canadian people are more interested in is whether the government commands a grasp of the problems facing the Canadian people, and whether the government has an effective program to deal with those problems.
Thus, I welcomed the amendment moved by my leader, because it brought the debate back to reality, back to the threat to Canadian independence created by growing foreign ownership of our economy. It brought us back to the reality of high levels of unemployment, to the reality of poverty and hardship that is being faced by many Canadian families.
If we heard something of the sublime in the Speech from the Throne and in the remarks of the Prime Minister, then I think we heard something of the ridiculous this afternoon from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). The Speech of the Minister of Finance this afternoon was a recitation of the failure of government policy. I noted that the minister placed a great deal of emphasis in his speech on laying the blame on the labour situation in Canada. It seemed to me that he was acting something like Dr. Young, Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission in this regard. I am not sure whether the Minister of Finance is parroting the chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission or whether the chairman is parro'.ing the minister; but in either case they are both talking in the same way.
For one thing, the minister commented on the wild gyrations taking place in the labour force participation rate. I suggest that this is just one more piece of evidence that points out that the government has a complete lack of control over the economic situation in Canada.
The minister took great pains to point out that there has been an increase in work stoppages in Canada. I think the key question is: Why are they taking place? The answer to the question is that the government

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Burton
has allowed a jungle-type society to continue to exist in this country. The government has failed to introduce a comprehensive incomes policy such as that proposed by New Democratic Party members. This is the reason for the increasingly difficult situation with respect to management-labour relations. Where is the incomes policy that we have heard suggested over the past several months?
The minister also said that a slowdown in wage demands is not coming. He suggested that this was the most important factor in the economy. On the other hand, he also pointed to a plunge in profits. I have never heard the minister express concern about a plunge in wages. Neither have I heard him express concern, or at least any great concern, for those Canadians who altogether lose their incomes as a result of unemployment. When did either the government or the Minister of Finance have any concern to express about the sharp increases in profits that have occurred during the past number of years? When did they have anything to say about the increase in interest rates? They have said nothing about that.
These factors are supposed to be indications of a healthy economy. Yet once wages start to go up this is cause for great concern amongst the government policy makers. This is why I suggest there is a basic contradiction involved here. I further suggest that the government has revealed its true colours in that it is not concerned with the ordinary working man in this country. Rather, it has concern for the corporate sector of the economy, for those people who already have a larger than proportionate share of the wealth of the country.
Certainly, the announcement of the minister this afternoon that more money would be voted to alleviate unemployment is belated but welcome. The minister then went on to say that a difficult winter is ahead. I suppose he expects people to take some consolation from that statement. He said that possibly there would be a return to normal growth conditions within the next four or five quarters.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that there will be a return to normal growth conditions at the end of 1971. The minister is suggesting that at that point it is possible the government will take steps to stimulate the economy. And what will happen near the end of 1971? This is very near the time when the government is going to think of calling the next federal election.
Both the Speech from the Throne and the Prime Minister's address dealt with economic conditions. There were curious contradictions and conflicts, some straying from the facts, and throughout a failure to face up to necessities and to the bankruptcy of government policy. On the one hand, it was noted that something had to be done about unemployment and other problems. On the other hand, the attitude of "I'm all right, Jack" was taken. At one point some satisfaction was gained from the contention that unemployment rates had levelled off. If it is suggested that the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at 6.7 per cent in both July and August of this year, this will be small consolation to many thousands of Canadians.
The situation was perfectly predictable. The government was warned from many sides that its economic policies would result in a serious slowdown in the Canadian economy. It was warned that the voluntary guidelines policy to be implemented by the Prices and Incomes Commission could not succeed. The New Democratic Party advocated a comprehensive incomes policy. Other proposals were advanced. But the government blindly persisted in its policies. Now, many thousands of Canadians are reaping the whirlwind of the government's policies.
The government is now faced with a serious problem. Expectations are for high unemployment this winter,- admitted by the minister-a serious slowdown in business investment and the prospect of no growth in the second half of 1970. It seems clear that there will be no real economic pick-up until well into 1971. The reason is obvious: there is a time lag between policy changes and their effect on the economy.
A year ago the New Democratic Party urged the government to change its policies. The government failed to listen. On Friday the leader of the New Democratic Party again put forward a five-point economic program involving public investment programs, investment controls, redistribution of income by tax reforms, prices and income controls if necessary, and action to reduce our dependence on and vulnerability to the United States economy.
The Speech from the Throne must be analysed in terms of its adequacy. No one will dispute that there are some welcome announcements in the Speech from the Throne and in subsequent statements by ministers. Some proposals may even be regarded as a faltering and inadequate step in the right direction. The establishment of ministries concerned with environmental affairs and urban affairs will be meaningful only if accompanied by sound, far reaching and courageous programs.
In the final analysis, the government's program must be judged on the basis of its adequacy. Does it take the necessary steps to ensure the well-being of Canadian society? Does it ensure the welfare of individual Canadians? Is it prepared to go beyond "equality of opportunity", as mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, to "equality of condition"? Does it show courage?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that on too many counts the government has fallen short in a speech liberally sprinkled with conflict and contradictions. Let me cite a few examples. According to the speech, the just society has now become the "distant ideal". Concern is expressed for the "life-support systems of the biosphere", and a new department of environmental affairs is to be created. But there is no assurance that the government is prepared to take the profound steps necessary to cope with these matters.
Reference is made to the need to anticipate and plan rather than reacting to events. But the government persists in taking smug satisfaction from its performance. Reference is also made to equality of opportunity, but not to equality of condition. Too often the phrase "equality of opportunity" is used in order to avoid the decisions necessary to bring about meaningful change. In reference to the government's urban activities, the Speech from the

October 13, 1970

Throne states that "the government seeks, by making rational its efforts in these fields", and so on. That is surely an admission of past irrationality and hardly an assurance of future common sense. Reference is made to the "competitive marketing system faced by consumers" and then we are told the government is going to do something about "combines, mergers and unfair trade practices".
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
There is only one short paragraph concerning problems of foreign ownership and no assurance of any program arising out of the current government study of this matter. The Speech from the Throne states:
It would be irresponsible to suggest that the economy is now in a satisfactory condition".
And then later:
Unemployment remains distressingly high in some parts of Canada-
It then concludes:
In sum, the vitality of the economy, coupled with present governmental policies, is countering slowly but effectively the pressures of inflation and unemployment.
Much lip service is paid to the United Nations. But words cannot make up for the failure of the Prime Minister to fulfil the expectation that he would address the 25th anniversary session of the UN on behalf of the people of Canada.
In the light of the two kidnappings in Montreal in the past ten days, special note must be taken of the statement in the Speech from the Throne:
Notwithstanding its difficulties, Canada continues to enjoy social stability to an exceptional degree.
Surely, this is the type of statement that can only contribute to an attitude of smug complacency which in turn allows situations to grow which eventually can result in the type of problems now faced by the governments of Canada and Quebec. It is not my intention to comment upon the immediate problems in view of the delicacy of the matter, but I did want to comment on some broader implications.
First, any tendency to donwngrade the problems facing Canadian nationhood is wrong. This crisis, which was somewhat submerged during the past year, now is a matter of concern for each and every Canadian. If we want a Canada we are going to have to work for it. For one, I want a Canada.
Second, the Prime Minister received a mandate from the Canadian people at the last election largely on the confidence and expectation that he could solve the problems of Canadian nationhood. Many people from all parts of Canada looked to him to save Canada. To create such a hope and expectation was false. To rely on such an approach was false. The evidence is now clear that, for whatever the reasons may be, the state of our nation has not improved and the Prime Minister has not reached the impossible objective associated with his political personality.
However, it would be folly to counsel despair. Rather, all Canadians must reassess the situation and develop
The Address-Mr. Burton
new approaches. Constitutional reform must be tackled on the basis of dealing with real issues and problems. Regional development programs must be related to people, not to the strengthening of private corporate power. Concepts of law and order must not be used as a weapon to prevent or hinder changes in outmoded or inadequate systems.
I was especially interested in the comments on tax reform in both the Speech from the Throne and the Prime Minister's speech, since I served as a member of the House committee studying the white paper. Members will know that the majority of the committee bowed to the pressure of business and corporate representations and recommended substantial concessions to the corporate sector. Maybe they did not go quite as far as the Senate committee but we really do not expect any better from the other place.
It is also noteworthy that the committee meekly acquiesced to the modifications of the Minister of Finance to the White Paper proposals as they affected the oil and mining industries. It might be useful to recall some events. On August 5, the minister informed the committee he did not intend to announce any further modification of the white paper but added a rider "you can never tell". On August 26, the minister announced his concessions. By early September, when the committee met to consider its report, government members were prepared to accept the new proposal without having asked a single question.
I note the Prime Minister attempted to rationalize the concession to the mining industry in terms of growth. I challenge him to reconcile these concessions with the statement in his speech last Friday, which reads, at page 34 of Hansard:
The only true prosperity is that which is equitably shared.
I challenge both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to reconcile these concessions with the following two sentences in the Speech from the Throne:
Thereafter, legislation will be introduced incorporating policies designed to make more equitable the economic burden shared by our fellow dwellers in this complex and varied land. These taxation measures are part of the government's pledge to utilize the wealth of Canada for the good of all Canadians and not just for those fortunate enough to be shielded by the protective apparatus of giant corporations, alert professional organizations or powerful labour unions.
This is one more example of the hollow words in the Speech from the Throne. It is one more piece of evidence that real tax reform is a long way off. While it now appears that the government intends to proceed with the enactment of whatever changes are finally decided upon, I hope adequate time will be reserved for consideration of the legislation.
Members will be aware that the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) and myself introduced a minority report on behalf of the New Democratic Party. I commend its recommendations to the Minister of Finance. Tax credits instead of tax exemptions, a full capital gains tax, an end to the special privileges associated with corporate and investment income, an end to special concessions to large oil and mining industries, integration of estate and income taxation, and an ade-

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Burton
quately structured progressive tax rate schedule-all of these things are needed for real tax reform.
The government must change its approach and not back down to the pressure of special interests. The Speech from the Throne correctly noted tensions existing in Canadian society. Inequality of wealth and economic power is one of the causes of these tensions. Failure on the part of the government to correct these inequalities can only intensify these tensions in society.
One final word on taxation concerning the provinces. There was some legitimate concern on the part of the provinces concerning the long run revenue implications for the provinces related to their fiscal needs. Beyond that the role played by the provinces in the White Paper debate was very disappointing. Most of the provinces joined the anguished cries of corporate business and were prepared to concede just about anything wanted. I think Canadians expected a more responsible approach by provincial governments. At least one provincial government has the unenviable position of being linked with the other place. A Leader-Post article dated October 1, 1970 is headed, "Province, Senate agree". The first paragraph reads:
The Saskatchewan government and the Senate Banking Committee see eye to eye in their disagreements with the federal government's white paper on tax reform.
I have already made some comments in respect of the national economic situation. I should now like to turn to a number of matters concerning the province of Saskatchewan which has been particularly hard hit by a combination of national economic events and special factors operating particularly in that province. The crisis faced by Saskatchewan during the past year poses many questions involving Saskatchewan's future and I would like to take a few minutes to discuss the implications of some government programs and policies on that future.
One indicator of the course of events in Saskatchewan is population. On July 1, 1970, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics estimated there were 940,000 people in Saskatchewan, an absolute drop of 22,000 from the figure of
962,000	in October, 1968. Net migration out of Saskatchewan would have of course been much higher. Unemployment figures have not reflected the true picture due to the high degree of mobility in Saskatchewan's labour force, the relatively high percentage of people engaged in agriculture and the fact that some groups, such as Indian people on reserves, are not included in labour force surveys.
Several industries have faced serious problems. Potash faced special problems due to unplanned, too rapid expansion; oil and uranium slowed down but most important, agriculture faced a real crisis due to a slow down in markets, price drops and continual cost increases. Agriculture is still the most important industry in Canada and grain production is still foremost within the industry. For this reason I think it is tragic that the Canada Grains Act was not passed at the last session. The government waited too long to introduce it with the result that we did not finish the committee stage until the last day before the summer adjournment. It was an improved bill that came out of the committee, and we in this party wanted the bill passed quickly. That was not
to be. When the House reconvened on October 5, the Conservative members tabled 44 amendments. I submit that such a move was made for one reason only, that was to kill the bill, and they did. Most of their amendments would have reduced the Grain Commission's powers to control the grain trade. Now, the bill has to be introduced again in this session before it will be possible to introduce protein grading which is so badly needed.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The Speech from the Throne tried to paint a good picture of the infamous Operation Lift and tried to suggest that it was responsible for unclogging wheat markets. I suggest that the unclogging of wheat markets was due more to crop conditions in a large number of foreign countries. It was also suggested that, the Lift program encouraged a healthy diversification of agricultural activities." Possibly the government has not heard that the price of weanling pigs in Saskatchewan dropped from $22 to $3 to $4 in recent months. Such are the consequences of crash programs like Operation Lift.
In addition, hon. members will recall that last spring the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board warned farmers not to increase their barley acreage. Some increase took place anyway. Now, we have the prospect of a barley shortage and the minister is busily covering his tracks by urging farmers to grow more barley.
In the long-run Operation Lift will prove a real setback to western Canadian agriculture. Had this expenditure been used to stabilize farm income, production adjustments would have been made without the damage that has been done.
Finally, it should be noted that when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) spoke last Thursday in the debate in seconding the motion now before us he did not once refer to Operation Lift, although he referred to many other items. From a farmer from a farm constituency in Saskatchewan, surely this silence is eloquent.
There are other aspects of agricultural problems in Saskatchewan that I would like to discuss, including price supports, marketing, grain movement, etc., but time does not permit. There is one particular matter though that is causing many farmers concern, that is the government's dairy policy.
I raise this matter because of the previously quoted reference claiming that Operation Lift encouraged agricultural diversification. Many farmers in Saskatchewan are concerned at the rigid application of the policies of the Dairy Commission which now effectively prohibit them from obtaining cream subsidies in particular. This operates badly for many prairie farmers because the Commission's policies were introduced at a time when grain markets were buoyant and many farmers had gone out of milk production. I hope the commission and the government will review the rules to bring about a more fair operation for any prairie farmers.
In answer to questions and representations the government has pointed out from time to time that Saskatchewan will benefit under regional development programs. Complaints have already been made about the low allocation of expenditures to Saskatchewan.

Why is Esk so much more stable than Serath? I have nothing against keeping Esk open, but let us compare the two communities.
Esk is about five miles from Lanigan, a rapidly growing town. Serath is about 20 miles from the nearest town. Serath has 50 householders according to the latest postal guide while Esk has 38. True, Serath does not have banking and medical facilities. What does Esk have? The 38 householders comprise 23 farmers, one teacher, three retired, one postmaster, four labourers, two grain agents, one carpenter, one housewife, one garage or service station operator, and one general-whatever that is.
The then Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) refused to listen to many representations and reasoning. Local Liberal politics held sway. Some local Liberal supporters wanted to get the rural route contract. This is the type of patronage politics that has hurt the post office more than all other factors. The two Liberal members from Saskatchewan played a disgraceful role in this episode.
Another matter of concern to many communities is the reduction in railway service. The CPR has closed most of its agencies in Saskatchewan, and branch line service in many areas is restricted to grain movement. Now, the CPR is trying to unload its last remaining passenger service in Saskatchewan, the main line service.
The CNR also tried to close most of its agencies and establish a master agency plan. Public reaction was so strong that it looks as if the CNR has called off its plans. Instead, it is resorting to the old railway game of squeezing out service when the railways do not get their way. Passenger tickets have been taken away from many station agents. Communities on some lines no longer have cartage services; draying contracts have been terminated; distribution of express is becoming more centralized. Such an approach by the railways is the height of irresponsibility.
These examples and many others I could cite, Mr. Speaker, illustrate how the structure of Saskatchewan communities is breaking down because of the lack of co-ordinated planning sensitive to the needs of people. What is needed in Saskatchewan is concern and attention to the needs of communities, large, small and rural, to ensure that viable communities exist which are desirable places for people to live, from aesthetic, cultural and economic standpoints.
Many program changes are needed. I give one small example. For years forest nursery stations have provided trees free of charge to farmers. A very useful service has been performed. I suggest the time has come when this service should also be provided to urban communities. I recognize that in doing so consideration would have to be given to the situation of commercial nurseries.
In view of the serious problems facing rural Canada and smaller communities, and in view of the urgent need for co-ordination, planning and programs I urge that a minister of state for rural affairs be appointed. A useful step will be taken by appointing a minister of state for urban affairs and housing. I hope this step will be followed by meaningful programs. I suggest there is a similar need for a minister of state for rural affairs. Because
of the failure of the government to act on this and many other problems, I will support the amendment to the amendment moved by the leader of the New Democratic Party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to congratulate the mover of the motion for the address in reply, the hon. member for Bourassa (Mr. Trudel), and the seconder, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas). I do this not only as a formality but because of my high personal esteem for both of these gentlemen.
Many years ago when I was a law student, I began to learn about the constitution of this great country. I learned pretty quickly that municipal institutions came under section 92 of the British North America Act, which meant they came under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Indeed, I had a very good teacher. My teacher in constitutional law was so eminent that he now sits as a justice on the Supreme Court of Canada.
Then, almost 20 years ago I went into municipal politics. I worked my way all the way up from nothing to a state of absolute poverty, through the stages of alderman and controller, and went on to become the mayor of my beloved city of Toronto. I saw the city of my birth grow from a population of 650,000 to a metropolitan area of over 2 million population. I saw it grow by an estimated
50,000	to 60,000 people a year each year for the past 20 years, and as well I saw grow its problems of congestion, poverty, housing, welfare, education, traffic jams and pollution. I saw these problems engulf my city and its environs.
Quite often I sat wringing my hands in frustration because of a lack of power and money to do the things which had to be done for my great city. I would go to the province with my hat in hand, like a mendicant or beggar, looking for financial assistance and legal assistance. I was told by the boys in the provincial government that it was the federal government which had the money and that I should go to see my friends in the federal government. So, I would come up to Ottawa. They would take me out to lunch and they would tell me, "Phil, you know very well that jurisdiction over the cities belongs to the provinces."
I rapidly became a track star on the run-around track of passing the buck, and when I came here as a federal member of Parliament two years ago I knew about the constitution. I knew what it said in the constitution but, Mr. Speaker, that did not make it right, because it did not accord with the reality of the situation.
I have argued loud and long, time and again, that the municipalities we now have in this great country are not the municipalities which were envisaged by the Fathers of Confederation and the BNA Act, that their responsibilities today are not just to fix curbs and fill potholes, to look after police protection and fire protection, that today the cities are conglomerates, and that Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver could never have been envisaged in 1867 in the extent to which they have grown today.
Indeed, notwithstanding the fact of the constitution, the federal government today is financially right up to its neck in municipal matters, to the extent of hundreds of

October 13, 1970

millions of dollars spent on housing, airports, harbours, post-secondary school education, post offices, public works and so on. Today the budgets of Montreal and Toronto are bigger than the budgets of at least seven of the provinces, and the populations of Montreal and Toronto are each bigger than the populations of seven of the provinces. Indeed, today the populations of each of the cities of Toronto and Montreal is bigger than the population of all the four Atlantic provinces put together.
If the provinces have a right to sit in at constitutional conferences, as I have seen them with premiers representing provinces which have populations of anywhere from 150,000 to 200,000 or 300,000 people, then surely the populations of our great cities have a right to be represented at these conferences which will determine the constitution of this country for the next 100 years.
I have pointed out that by the year 1980-this has been stated time and again by eminent statisticians and research authorities-which is only a short ten years off, 80 per cent of the population of Canada will be living in the cities of the nation. Sixty per cent of our population will be living in cities of over 100,000 population, and one third of the entire population of the nation will be living in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. I have argued that there was a need for the federal government to manifest its concern for the cities in order to prod the provinces, even though the cities are their responsibility under the constitution, something which I have never denied. I have argued that urban areas have affected national policies, financial and monetary policies, more than many of the provinces. In any event, Mr. Speaker, we are not dealing with municipalities as such but with people, the people we represent in this House of Commons.
But, Mr. Speaker, all these arguments seemed to fall on deaf ears. I was told that the constitution stood in the way, that I was beating my head against a brick wall, and so it seemed to me.

speechtext:
Anyway, I will leave to others the chronicling of the sequence of events which took place from the beginning, two years ago, until now. But, lo and behold, in the Throne Speech last week my impossible dream seems to have come true. By the appointment of a secretary of state for urban affairs and housing, the government has acknowledged that it has a place in the urban affairs of the nation. This is a specific acknowledgement in the Throne Speech. This is a de jure as well as a de facto recognition that the federal government owes responsibility, and is manifesting its concern, for the cities. It could not be clearer than it is in the Throne Speech. This means to me that there will now be a recognition of the place of municipal governments in the day to day public business of this country and in the planning for the future. In addition, in the search for a new Canadian constitution, the municipalities will be recognized and accepted as participating partners and be given a role consistent with their influence on the lives of the Canadian people.
The Address-Mr. Givens
So far as I am concerned I consider this to be a total vindication of my position and I have only one word of caution I wish to express at this time. If a federal initiative in urban affairs is to bear fruit, it must necessarily be accepted in good faith and must take into account the indispensable participation of the other levels of government, particularly in the area of formulation of national urban policies. It must be a tri-partite arrangement. This means that the federal government must recognize and pursue actively its responsibility to foster effective and continuous consultation between all levels of government in the formulation of national urban policies. It also means that the municipal governments must recognize the responsibility they have to consult together in the formulation of the municipal point of view. They must, themselves, come to terms with the problems that are situate within their boundaries and they must work together to assure a better understanding by each municipality and its officials of national urban problems. Without the full participation of municipalities as provincial and national groupings any federal initiative is doomed to failure. Without the full and active participation of individual provinces and the provinces as a group, once more federal initiative is doomed to failure.
The Canadian municipalities, through the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, have obviously contributed to the alerting of the federal government to its need to take an initiative in urban affairs. Let us hope that the municipalities do not consider the federal initiative to be a sufficient measure. Let us hope that they are urged to move even further and faster along the road to three party consultation rather than make the fatal mistake-and this is what it would be-of relaxing their efforts at the first sign of success in this venture.
Much has been said about the matter of pollution. We have been inundated with a miasma of pollution jargon. In an age of transcience in which fashions and fads change over night, as people leap from one sensation to another, there is a strong danger that the public will lose interest and that the destruction of our environment will continue apace as man goes the way of the dinosaur into oblivion. But I do not think this will happen.
I think that pollution is, and will continue to be, the vital issue for the rest of this century. If we fail in this period of time and over the next generation to control its disastrous devastation and to repair the basic defects of rampant population growth and uncontrolled technology, and if we do not somehow adjust our concern about the environment and adapt it to our traditional institutional framework of society, then we will have had it; we simply will not survive. Many cracks have been made by sophisticated, "hep", people, the swingers, who have wondered out loud through the facilities of the media whether the furore about pollution is full of sound and fury signifying nothing and whether indeed it is a passing fad like the mini or the midi or the Nehru jacket. There are the neanderthal types in all walks of life who have indicated that it is only a tempest in a teapot, a gimmick for professors and radical students to attract attention and publicity for themselves.
In the past decade we have seen many emotional and volatile issues grab people and shake them only to be

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Givens
forgotten the day after tomorrow. Our attention span is terribly short and our concentration as fickle as a femme. This unfortunately is true. I feel, however, that never before have we been faced with an issue of such vital significance to ourselves and the future of our children and our grandchildren. This is an issue which we live with every day and which is before our very eyes day in and day out, week in and week out, year after year. We are reminded of it constantly as we breathe the air, listen to the constant cacaphony of deafening noises around us, struggle through crowds and traffic, twitch our noses and turn away from looking at the streams, rivers and lakes in and out of our cities in order to keep from throwing up.
If in the face of these frightening reminders which we see every day we turn away or lose interest and turn to something else for kicks, then we will truly deserve the catastrophe which will descend on our heads. Therefore, I consider the call in the Throne Speech for a co-ordination and consolidation of all our efforts in an effective fashion and the establishment of a department with a mandate for the protection of the biosphere to be a declaration of major importance which would not have been possible two years ago.
On the subject of abortion, I welcome the proposal for a special debate. Naturally, I would prefer to see the government take specific action on this matter but two years in these hallowed halls and corridors have taught me that there are many deep and serious divisions of opinion on this subject and of course I have mine. I do not think I will ever forget the debates in this House when we were discussing the therapeutic abortion amendment to the Criminal Code omnibus bill last year.
The state of New York, which has a population greater than the whole of Canada and which has an ethnic, racial and religious mix which is a microcosm of the whole of the United States and comparable to ours, has freed abortion from criminal strictures. Although this great state is just across the border, it may as well be at the other end of the world so far as this progressive move is concerned. At least the xenophobes in our midst can take comfort in the fact that we have not been brainwashed and acculturated to this degree by our United States neighbour.
When we passed the therapeutic abortion amendment I really believed we had done a good thing and that we would be protecting about 100,000 Canadian women a year who seek illegal abortions from the back alley butchers who prey on them. Alas, this has not been the case. I believe it is time this Parliament took heed of the growing number of Canadians who maintain that an intimate decision concerning abortion should be made by the woman or couple concerned, without being dominated by those who would impose their ideas concerning morality and religion on others who hold entirely different views and beliefs.
I feel the same way about another controversial matter mentioned in the Throne Speech. I refer to the question of the non-medical use of drugs. I have been appalled by what I have seen in the courts in Toronto and by what is going on in the courtrooms throughout this nation with regard to this problem. Every day hundreds of youths
across this country are being arrested, mugged, finger printed and given a criminal record at the start of their lives for the mere possession of a "reefer" or two of Cannabis marijuana. Many of these kids have come from our finest homes. The result of such conviction, regardless of the penalty imposed by enlightened courts, has a devastating effect on the families as well as the accused. It is granted that this whole problem in respect of drugs is vexing and perplexing, but this method of handling these cases under the Criminal Code is really archaic and Draconian in an enlightened society. I shall anxiously await the commission's final report so that it can be studied, discussed and acted upon without further delay.
So, for the reasons I have indicated, I am delighted with the Throne Speech and for the first time in the two years I have been here I can honestly say I now feel at home in this House.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take the opportunity of congratulating the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne (Mr. Trudel and Mr. Douglas).
We are all invited to discuss the Speech from the Throne. In all such speeches, we find valuable items and some that are less so, as well as omissions. This speech teems with good intentions. In fact, it says, and I quote:
As Canada moves into the seventies, we are ail invited to join in this bold enterprise-to share the excitement, to face the challenge, to pursue the distant ideal of a just society.
Further, it says:
The Canada of the seventies must continue to be a land for people; a country in which freedom and individualism are cherished and nurtured; a society in which the Government lends its strength to withstand, rather than support the pressures for conformity.
That surely set me wondering! Here is more:
Fortunately, our population, the number of Canadians engaged in productive employment, the total volume of goods and services which they produce, and Canadian exports all continue to grow.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to spend the few minutes I have left commenting only the Throne speech. As many others, I would like to make some objective remarks.
After two years in the House, we might well ask ourselves certain questions. In fact, there were 300,000 unemployed two years ago; today there are 500,000 people out of work.
The government has adopted an anti-inflationary policy. The attempt to limit salary increases to 6 per cent is an example. However, they forgot to ask industries and businesses to restrict their profits to 6 per cent. To me, it was gross injustice. I was very surprised to see that the government wanted to limit salary increases to 6 per cent without any consideration for low wage earners. This type of unfairness was designed to widen the gap between the rich and the poor.
As regards housing, there are still very serious problems in this field.
On many occasions-and I shall take the liberty of repeating this-we had asked the Minister to repeal the
[Mr. Givens.l
October 13, 1970

11 per cent sales tax on building materials. For a year and a halt now, we have been asking the government to make low-interest loans to workers with low incomes. In my view, such action would soon bring about the expansion of the construction industry.
A policy aimed at making the repayment of loans easier may well be introduced, still, low-income workers cannot be required to pay over the years three times the actual value of their homes.
It is indeed a pleasure and a duty to request once again-and I hope the minister will listen to us this year-low-interest loans, or, in other words, loans bearing interest at 5 or 6 per cent for wage-earners with an annual income of $10,000 or less.
With respect to agriculture, the two years that have just elapsed have not yet brought the expected profits of results. This could be discussed at length. However, where the milk producers are concerned and taking into account their good faith in relation with quotas, I urge the minister in charge to rectify as quickly as possible the iniquities they have been suffering s.nce last April. Because of that iniquitous situation-and many of you know it-several dairy farmers have disappeared. The minister had undertaken to put an end to that anomaly as soon as the good faith of the dairy farmers could be established. Having said this I hope that the minister will act without any delay so that these producers can get the grants they need desperately. We have perhaps forgotten during the last two years to readjust the pensions of the blind and the disabled. Those pensions set at $75 monthly are insufficient, and this has been the case for a long time. I hope that this year we will be able, after discussion, to increase the pension of the people who, in addition to living alone, need someone to help them. This $75 pension, in view of the need for a companion, is ridiculous surely, considering the cost of living today. Since April 1964, a blind person cannot earn more than $1,600 a year or his pension will be reduced. I hope the government will reconsider this measure and will allow a blind man to become less dependent and thanks to his skill, to increase his income without losing his pension.
Mr. Speaker, if we make a quick survey, it is hard to believe that we will gain the confidence of the people in this manner.
Last year, I spoke at some length about objectivity. I thought that, which the good will of all hon. members, we could achieve a greater degree of objectivity, act more as administrators than as politicians. Such objectivity, I feel, has not been exercised in the manner that I and the whole population of Canada would have wished to see in the House. This year, I hope that there will be more objectivity here than heretofore. We can never gain the confidence of the people so long as suggestions brought forward and likely to help our fellow-citizens are being rejected.
I dare hope that we may still prove our Parliament to be truly democratic.
To my way of thinking party discipline is much too rigid in certain cases.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I know that the party in power is often embarrassed. I also know that, according to an old tradition, any legisla-
The Address-Mr. La Salle
tion introduced in the House, if rejected, necessarily brings about the fall of the government.
In my view, this tradition could disappear. I feel that the government should be defeated through a vote of non-confidence. If this measure were more clearly defined we could ask the political parties to be less rigid when party discipline is involved.
I do not accept very well that party discipline should involve the conscience of the members, because this practice leads us to deny certain commitments we have made and forces us to vote against our own convictions. Obviously, the party in power is often placed before this dilemma. By changing that attitude or those old traditions, we could give more freedom to the members and thereby prove to the Canadian people that a democratic parliament can really be achieved.
As long as party discipline is that rigid, it will continue to bind the conscience of the members. There are striking examples.
Indeed, last spring, the matter of dairy policy came up.
I remember full well that the majority of the members, who represent rural areas, were not in favour of the government policy. But the party discipline was strong enough to silence the members of the party in power and the government cut back the subsidies by $10 million, which did excessive harm to milk producers.
Today, we are still trying to get the situation back to normal. But the fact remains that party discipline forced a number of members to vote, I am convinced, against their convictions. They would have liked to have fought for the interests of the riding they promised to represent well, but they were unable to do so.
Now, I dare hope changes will be made to that effect, to enable Parliament to allow all its members to be more honest and honour their commitments towards their electors.
Mr. Speaker, a while ago mention was made of a bill allowing greater freedom in the matter of abortions. I am sorry that the Speech from the Throne did not refer to a bill that would have given us the opportunity of discussing abortion this year. I feel that the impressive statistics published in the last three years and a half justify a new debate on that law.
I would have liked better during this session to see a debate on capital punishment rather than on further liberalization of the legislation on abortion. I would have preferred that we should try to get rid of our criminals rather than consider doing away with innocent people.
Mr. Speaker, I shall take this opportunity to mention a problem of some significance in my riding which does not have only advantages but also its own problems.
For the past few months I have made representations to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) in order to get, on behalf of my riding, information concerning the current unemployment rate. I consider myself justified in asking the minister for a better understanding of the difficulties we experience at this time.
There are various reasons for the 15 per cent unemployment rate in my riding. We should also be able to find work for some 1,500 students who enter the labour market each year.

The Address-Mr. La Salle
The training programmes that have been made necessary by the work done at the international airport and that normally should help reduce unemployment will certainly not be felt before 1980. As there were reductions in some areas of the textile industries in my constituency, unemployment has gained momentum.
I am convinced that the minister understands the situation and that he will attempt to give it special attention. I will have the opportunity in the near future to present him with a petition from my constituency, namely from all the municipalities, the Chambers of Commerce, the Regional Economic Council and from cities such as Joliette and l'Assomption. I think that, in the light of claims which will show the difficulties we are experiencing, the minister will seriously consider the possibility of including my constituency as a designated region or at least setting up special areas which would be a great help for us.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about severe unemployment throughout Canada and particularly in the province of Quebec.
I made on occasions some suggestions aimed at curtailing unemployment. There are works to be done in each municipality. I wonder whether we could not ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government to give special attention to the organization of winter works this year. This is something that was going on previously, but that has been called off by the government. I wonder whether we would not have reasons re-establish them, at least with respect to public services in each municipality.
I wonder also whether it would not be desirable to have students work during the summer at cleaning up our waterways; this would give employment to students and help fight pullution at the same time.
These works would confer a tourstic attraction to our cities.
I would like to ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion as well, to consider very particularly the possibility of granting assistance to industries.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has greatly improved the situation by allowing certain expenses in different areas of Canada, especially in the province of Quebec. We have, therefore, profited by a reasonable part of those works.
But I wonder if it is adequately considered to protect the industries. It is very interesting to see a certain number of new industries come into being, but I believe that we unfortunately forget to give them adequate attention. In my opinion, it would be much less burdensome to allow these industries to have a certain expansion or, at least, to continue their operations.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to say a few words on a question which has not been mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, namely the measure to amend the constitution. Some hon. members talked about the matter and discussed it, but I regret that that question has not received the priority which it deserves.
I think that in the opinion of Quebecers and of all other Canadians, such a change is becoming increasingly essential and should have been mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. People are worried right now because
October 13, 1970
we are living anguishing hours. Still, I believe we should ask what is behind this phenomenon.
I think that over the past 10 years Quebec has made quite normal claims at federal-provincial conferences. Perhaps the federal government has refused for too long to recognize the particular situation of Quebec in Canada. In fact, 80 per cent of Quebec's population is nevertheless represented by French speaking people.
The history of the French Canadian nation leads us to recognize differences. It is also the responsibility of Quebec to see to the preservation of our traditions, of our turn of mind and of our views which are not necessarily identical to those of other Canadians. I think that these are quite rightful aspirations. We share much in common with all other Canadians: we want well-being and affluence but, at the same time, we want to keep our language and our habits, desires which are quite legitimate.
I regret, however, that the federal government should be reluctant to revise the Constitution, which discourage, to a certain extent a number of Quebec people. It may be that the federal members from the Province of Quebec should have given their colleagues from the other provinces more precise information on the difficulties and the aspirations of Quebecers. It may have been to often said that only a few people, a gang of bums, were involved, and that the matter did not have any great importance.
If that is so, then it was not the truth. A wish for emancipation was coming alive in Quebec. I believe that, to a certain extent, it was due to some hesitation in granting this wish that the movement for independence came into being, and, through all this, it happens that some groups go further than those who wish to remain peaceful.
Some will say that at the last election, the Province of Quebec, being well satisfied with the present system, elected a majority government which favoured federalism. But perhaps no attention was drawn to the fact that 66 per cent of the French-speaking population of Quebec voted for opposition parties, and this proves the dissatisfaction of a large number of citizens.
I say that because we already have a committee whose very first task will be to tackle the problem of improving the constitution.
I also believe that the briefs submitted by the Quebec governments since 1960 were aiming at the same goal and emphasizing the needs of the whole Canadian population.
The brief tabled at the last conference was almost the same as those from the precedent governments although its tune was a little different.
If on occasion we have perhaps changed our tune, it might be because we used the appropriate tune at the time, which made it possible for the Quebec premier to change his tune and perhaps his words while still taking into consideration Quebec's objectives and needs and also the conditions by which this province could remain in our great country, Canada, so that the Quebec people could be happier and more content.
I do not think that by passing one single piece of legislation we could settle the problem of national unity.
I believe in differences. Some are found in our province

October 13, 197 0

but also elsewhere. We are prepared to recognize them and we have proved it.
Should we also ask to the majority oi hon. members to understand these differences in order that each citizen can get his share of happiness and satisfaction in Canada?
We are willing to accept-and we have proved it-the differences that exist in other provinces. I must say that so that there can be a better understanding in our country, since I am convinced that, if we were better informed and more open-minded, we would be able not only to accept the province of Quebec, but to keep it within Canada and to make it easier for it to obtain the particuler rights which would enable its inhabitants to be happy. Under these conditions, we will build our country-and this is surely the desire of the vast majority of Quebecers-while respecting the differences existing not only in Quebec but elsewhere as well.
After all, I still think that in the future, thanks to a better understanding from those sitting here, the province of Quebec will develop further in this beautiful country which is called Canada.
