speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the next few minutes I should like to express my opinion on the Speech from the Throne delivered on October 8. I commend the government for it because I am convinced that its devoted civil servants must have taken a lot of time to prepare as perfect, as eloquent a piece of oratori-al art as this with such high-sounding but absolutely meaningless words.
In my estimation, this speech could easily be compared to a stuffed animal. One admires the art of the craftsman who has given it an appearance so near to reality; one admires the finish, even the elegance of this so-called work of art, but everyone knows very well there is no consistency inside this beautiful body, that this lovely decor hides only a few pounds of straw and that the whole thing rests on the ability of the craftsman to give it its striking appearance.
Once again, as usual, we are given pompous statements devoid of meaning.
Mr. Speaker, one reads in the Speech, and I quote:
Canada continues to enjoy social stability to an exceptional degree.
Incidentally, I should like to say that when the Speech from the Throne was written our situation was not what it is today. Still, we knew something was wrong. Today, the situation is far more serious than we thought.
They dare say that Canada enjoys exceptionoal social stability. I wonder where the staff of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) get their information.
Perhaps the people working for some of the hon. opposites still believe in Santa Claus. If the members of the government believe in Santa Claus, I beg of them to dispense with trying to make us believe in him. Obviously, we no longer do.
The Address-Mr. Beaudoin
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, someone should ask the employees of G. Lapalme Inc. if they believe in Santa Claus! We should ask the farmers of Eastern Canada if they are still expecting Bill C-197 from Santa Claus! Western farmers who are at grips with the famous Lift program should be asked if they think Santa Claus exists! We should also ask Canadian shoe manufacturers, Indians of the North, as well as foreign investors whether they believe in Santa Claus!
In one word, Mr. Speaker, government members should leave their offices and look around.
If the Prime Minister's statement is true, what are we doing here? If everything is fine, why keep trying to improve the situation? We are now at the beginning of the third test year of the present government which is repeating its usual story, the establishment of its just society.
I sincerely wonder if it is a just society for fun or a just society for a few. According to the Winnipeg Free Press of April 21 last, Governor Louis Rasminsky of the Bank of Canada stated that average salary increases of 7 to 8 per cent a year too high to allow the federal government to successfully combat inflation.
Well, in the course of last year, no doubt as an active participation in the anti-inflation fight, this same Mr. Rasminsky raised his own salary from $50,000 to $75,000 a year, or 50 per cent, which is only six or seven times more than what he had considered too high. A just society for whom, Mr. Speaker?
I am not against the principle of "just" salary increases. I use the word according to the meaning it has for us Creditistes, that is, equal justice for all.
Justice demands, I claim, that the wage increases to be granted to Canadian workers be proportionally equal to that given to Mr. Rasminsky.
But you will say that this would be absolutely impossible, and you are right. Then why not keep wages at a stationary level and cut down commodity prices? Impossible again, you will reply. And again I agree; such action is impossible in this unhealthy system. The solution to the problem lies in the implementation of Social Credit policies.
I know for sure that nobody will ever accept this truth without being compelled to do so. And in spite of it all, it is considered that Canada enjoys exceptional social stability. Words! Words! Words! Preposterous I say!
Where is that so-called just society? Are we talking about true distributive justice, or about the hollow concept of "justice"? Speaking of "justice", I think that at the present moment, we know nothing about it in Canada.
I would like, at this stage, to relate a conversation I had with somebody whose logic was perplexing.
In view of all that is happening in Canada, this person asked me simply: "Why should the federal government not decide to be honest once and for all and enact legislation which would confiscate to the benefit of the government all private property in Canada?*

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Beaudoin
This person told me that he considered the present governments as true usurpers taxing indispensable commodities in order to take over, by indirect means, what belongs to the people.
Why not, then, frankly be usurpers and do it directly, without hiding behind taxes? What do you answer to such advanced logic? In my opinion, such a statement leads us to doubt the exceptional social stability we enjoy in Canada, according to the Speech from the Throne.
Every day there are edifying news about attempts made to bring about a just society. Thus, in looking through the annual report of the Canadian Film Development Corporation for 1969-70 I was quite surprised to find out that such films as L'lnitiation and Les deux femmes en or had received financial assistance from the said corporation.
Mr. Speaker, here is what it says on page 9, and I quote:
"Under Section 10(2) of the Act establishing the Corporation, a completed film, in order to be eligible for a grant, must have a significant Canadian content.
Mr. Speaker, it is conceivable that a producer could decide to include in a film obscenities, insults to justice, words that vilely sully the beliefs of the majority of Canadians, and all sorts of things we all, I am sure, condemn, since he alone assumes moral and financial responsibility for them.
But that taxes paid by Canadians should contribute to the financing of such films, that, I repeat, is revolting to me. I strive to bring my children up in the natural respect of genuine love and of the most elementary human values, hereas the government, using funds raised from the fruit of my labours and those of all Canadians, allows producers to show such films in all our movie houses, accompagnied by spectacular and well-orchestrated publicity. That, Mr. Speaker, is beyond my understanding and I am squarely against it.
Is this the "just society" which means to shake the foundations of a self-respecting society? We should not wonder at the trouble our young people have been giving us lately. And to think that in the report it is said that such movies have a significant Canadian content. Supported, I suppose, by some kind of foundation garment. Is this what should be used to identify our society, as basic principle? Perhaps it is one of the objectives sought in the creation of the "just society"!
Moreover, we are spending thousands of dollars to find the reasons why so many young people take drugs. In fact, we are degrading them with all kinds of things and they have no hope left in the future.
There is no logic in the government's attitude, Mr. Speaker. Thousands of dollars are spent on research into the harmful effects of cigarettes, drugs, etc., and at the same time, tobacco farmers are granted subsidies to increase their production. As for me, I do not really see the logic in such a reasoning on the part of a government deemed reasonable.
We can also see in the Speech from the Throne that the government has just found a miracle solution to the problem of housing and pollution by establishing federal
departments. We really feel that the matter is being dealt with, that we need no longer worry about housing and pollution. The creation of these departments is so ridiculous that it is virtually impossible to say a word about it to our constituents without making them laugh, and I do understand them!
This reminds me of the fine books and documents that I keep preciously on the shelves in my office, here, in the parliament buildings. They all deal with bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada. So many words which mean nothing.
In my opinion, bilingualism in Ottawa is, in fact, a French Canadian who speaks English.
Most of the messengers of the House of Commons, whose mother tongue is French, speak English, while those whose mother tongue is English are very seldom able to speak French. The same applies to elevator operators, members of the protective staff, etc. And yet large amounts of money are used to publish rubbish submitted by young people who are not much more intelligent than their proposals.
What is the use of special commissions, task forces and even departments, when we know very well that this will in no way change the views of our devoted Prime Minister? Where is the democracy of which we have been hearing for 20 years? We should call this a dictatorship, because here in Ottawa, there is only one man who governs. We see this every day. I am thinking of the worthwhile efforts of hon. members who sit on committees and of the reports of which no account is ever taken.
* (4:40 p.m.)
We are informed of a possible series of debates on consumer protection, reorganization of the textile industry and the study of the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, etc. Even people outside politics could easily see, upon reading the speech, that the present government is beating around the bush to save time. The Prime Minister is the only one who knows what the immediate future of the country will be.
The uneasiness we are plagued with is an economic one. All efforts to protect the consumer, to reorganize the textile industry and to raise unemployment benefits, will have to be made all over again soon if we do not change the foundation of our economic system.
And the foundation I am talking about here is that of the monetary concept.
Mr. Speaker, it is amazing to note how easily certain people get lost in the clouds. In conclusion to his brilliant speech, our clear-sighted Prime Minister stated, and I quote:
We stand on the threshold of greatness.
I am convinced that this sentence will remain famous in our records for posterity. It is about the 30th time that at the opening of a session of Parliament, our poetically-minded prime ministers have really felt they stood on the threshold of greatness. This is where we have been standing for the last 100 years. What a joke!

October 13, 1970

Extreme poverty exists in the St. James district, in my riding. People there no longer believe in beautiful and bombastic tirades.
We must put an end to this once and for all.
Some government members may tell me that this time, it is for good that our poetically-minded Prime Minister is truly on the threshold of greatness.
This has been said so often that I feel people like us should not let ourselves be forever taken in by the same thing.
For the last few days, we have been living in the climate which prevails on the other side of that threshold. For my part, I do not believe that it is the threshold of greatness. The people who are active in the FLQ are surely to be condemned, and I condemn them very strongly. Actions such as those taken recently should, in my opinion, be most severely punished. However, I do understand them! For quite a long time, especially in Quebec, certain demands have been made, and, as long as the authorities do not get their arm twisted, nobody will do anything. We are floundering about in a completely obsolete system. The poor are telling us that. It is most difficult for a student, a small wage earner to work and survive.
The government is resorting to handsomely paid publicity to fool the people. It is using funds coming out of the tax-payers' pockets to finance pornographic films. It sets up inquiry commissions by the dozen without achieving any results. Their reports are only so many beautiful books. Furthermore, it is claimed that our country enjoys "social stability to an exceptional degree" and that we are "on the threshold of greatness."
Let us put the question to some 1,500 businessmen or others who went bankrupt this year in the province of Quebec. It will be seen if we have reached the threshold of greatness, especially the threshold of prosperity.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks, I want to assure the hon. members that as long as I have the privilege to make my views known in this House, I shall do so with vigour and determination in an attempt, against all hope, to bring them to open their eyes and see the "greatness" on the threshold of which we are standing, a greatness that wallows in violence, in a total lack of respect for the fundamental rights of society, in the tolerance of all known vices, in the recognition of the greatest agitators in the world, among other things.
I want future generations to know that it will not be people like me or my colleagues who will have brought this so-called just society, this so-called greatness but the present so-called government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) told us a few minutes ago that the Speech from the Throne was a mere list of good intentions. Knowing him and having spoken with him at noon, I feel he is attaching a derogatory meaning 'o the words "good intentions".
The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc
I also believe that a Speech from the Throne should represent a program being implemented by people, as a team, with good intentions.
First, I want to congratulate the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne (Mr. Trudel and Mr. Douglas) who carried out their task with sincerity and conviction.
In the hon. member for Bourassa, I have recognized the realistic businessman who is used to aim straight at the target and speaks his mind.
In the other mover, the member from Assiniboia, I have recognized a most serious man, with a sense of humour which is a quality we should keep if we really want to be objective and positive in our daily tasks.
The member form Assiniboia spoke with great competence on the agricultural problem, all the more so since all hon. members and many Canadians are aware that he is in a position to speak as an expert on agriculure as he is himself a master in this field.
During the few minutes at my disposal, I propose to express my own modest opinion on the opposition's motions, which I would call negative, and to state why I fully support the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I am opposed to the opposition's motions. The subamendment of the New Democratic Party, for instance, states in the first place that the government failed to deal effectively with the threat to Canadian independence which is dear to all of us.
However, I believe that the government did take effective measures to protect the economic independence of our country.
I believe we could give a lot of examples to substantiate this statement, but I intend to mention just one: the industrial incentives legislation which has been improved over the past few years and which has been most beneficial in our areas, especially in mine where employment was provided.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Besides, the government intends to take further steps in this connection. For instance, the bill on the uranium industry with regard to foreign control is a concrete example of what is contained in the Speech from the Throne as to the government's program.
When I speak of negative attitudes, I have in mind certain positions taken by the New Democratic Party and, as a case in point, I will mention a topic which is of particular interest to us from the lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe region.
I have in mind a debate on a private bill concerning the population of low-wage earners of my region, the Quebec Telephone bill regarding the Compagnie de telephone Bonaventure et Gaspe Limitee.
Members of the New Democratic Party did not allow representatives of the latter company to appear before Parliament and expound the situation. And those people talk about freedom and democracy. When people wish to come and explain what they want to do for the citizens

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc
of my area, they are not allowed to speak. Our friends of the New Democratic Party did that!
The New Democrat subamendment deals with the high rate of unemployment. According to that party, the government has not done anything. But we all know that the government has set a policy to reduce unemployment. I mean the professional training and retraining as well as the Canada Manpower Mobility program.
Every day many unemployed Canadians benefit from this program and from retraining courses. I know that education, curriculum preparation and complete jurisdiction in education comes under the provinces.
However there is nothing to prevent us, economically speaking, from encouraging our young people and our unemployed citizens to complete their education, their training.
As mentioned in the Speech from the Throne and as all Canadians can see for themselves, inflation which has been a very serious problem, not only in Canada but in many other countries, is on the wane.
The fight against inflation has not helped the government to deal with the problems of unemployment but, with inflation decreasing, we can hope it will be easier for the government and for all citizens to work on bringing down the high rate of unemployment.
The government intends to continue its action to this end. We will just mention the various regional development agreements the government plans to revise or renew. And we could mention many other steps the government intends to take.
The sub-amendment also deals with the guaranteed minimum income, in order to abolish the poverty from which at least five million Canadians are said to be suffering. We are all for it, because all of us want to carry on the fight against poverty.
However, it would be a mistake to say that this government has done nothing or is doing nothing to ensure a minimum income to Canadian citizens, because that is what it has been trying to do since 1968.
Take the social programmes that have been improved and will be further improved. Let us also consider the efforts made by the Economic Council of Canada in order to advise Parliament, the government and the Canadian people. And the government wishes to continue to guarantee such an income since a measure to that effect stands in the name of the government.
At this stage, I should like to add a personal remark. When it comes to providing an income, we must also think of providing jobs, and since the people are willing to work, it may be more practical, and we would thus perhaps show more consideration for the pride of our fellow-citizens, to take steps to find them jobs.
And I come now to the amendment in the name of the official opposition. It states in part, and I quote:
-of the indecision and the failure of Your Excellency's advisers-[DOT]
In my humble opinion, there has been no indecision nor have there been failures.
If we consider realistically the 1968 program, without thinking of any Christmas gifts for Santa Claus, as the previous speaker mentioned, it may be said that it has been completed.
The idea of a balanced budget was put forward. Certain steps have been undertaken in order to balance the budget, and I believe that all Canadians will agree on that point.
At that time, the government made it known to us that it wanted first to pass the bills under consideration by this House, which we have done.
The new program shows the good-will of the government. The negative approach of the opposition can also bring about failures. I think of the famous Bill C-197 which the previous speaker mentioned. That legislation, which was designed to aid farmers and to make trade easier between the provinces has now been studied for months. Even during the period of adjournment, the members of the committee came back to consider that bill. Why? In order to be able to pass it during the session which ended a few days ago. And I think that the provincial authorities were hoping that we would adopt that measure before the end of the last session. It turned out to be a failure.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The destructive opposition makes of the just society which is proposed a remote ideal. When one speaks of an "ideal" one always thinks of something that must be relatively far-off. Far-off, yes, but where and in what place? It is, in fact, the same ideal that individuals and societies have always wished to attain, a purpose that is relatively far-off. A program such as the one contained in the Speech from the Throne represents, it seems to me, the research for a far-off ideal.
In 1968, the government has spelled out his "philosophy" of the just society. I use this word even if some members have used it in a disparaging sense. Someone said it was time to live through justice and not off charity, and to do everything possible to achieve a just society. I fail to see why the opponents of the government, the members of the other parties, should chide the government or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for speaking to us of a just society. Its achievement is not the promise of Santa Claus, or the promise of a miracle for tomorrow, because no one can tell us today that, tomorrow, we will have a just society. However, someone who is sincere can promise to use all the means at his disposal to achieve a just society. We can, for instance, even today, make an ideal of our concept of a just society and the Speech from the Throne, according to me, is a proof of that.
As a whole, I think the attitude of the opposition is negative. I am proud to express my views on behalf of my electors of the riding of Rimouski. That negative attitude of the opposition is surely harmful. That it should harm our party, in the face of the problems now facing us, has no importance.
Some time ago I read that a statesman must work for the generations to come but that a politician, in the narrow sense of the word, works solely towards the next

October 13, 1970

elections. To my mind, some members of the opposition could meditate upon that statement. Such an attitude is harmful to the good features of our system, and it is certainly harmful to parliament which is the expression of our freedom, and a tool that has proved itself and will continue to do so provided we can continue to improve it.
I feel that attitude has lessened the confidence Canadians have in the system, in parliament. That is why I think it might be wise for the opposition, instead of acting as it has done in the last few days, instead of refusing to see what is good in the program of the Liberal party, and saying that it is all wrong, that the government achieves nothing, to at least admit that there are good things in the Speech from the Throne which, as I said a while ago, illustrates a philosophy and a program.
Everyone will agree, I hope, that it is quite normal to bring to mind certain principles, to say why we want to work towards this or that end, before preparing a program like that one.
Philosophy and program, both are necessary since it is impossible that everything can be bad and, in line with this, I will refrain from adopting the extreme standpoint of our friends in the opposition. When I tell them that they find everything bad, I do not suggest that all is fine in Canada, which would be naive from me. In fact, some problems do require a solution in this country, and this is a truism. This is why we should always have governments and other structures designed to solve our problems, such as that of the Constitution for instance. It is said that the government is ignoring it, but a special joint committee has been created by this House to make a survey of all the constitutional issues which have been discussed for years.
The question of tax reform is dealt with in the famous white paper which has been talked about so much lately. We all have fears, in spite of the committee report published recently. We think it right that the small wage-earner will no longer have to pay taxes in future, if legislation is passed accordingly. But we believe that the load of the middle class should be lightened, because middle class people work very hard to maintain the economic stability of this country. It seems to us that there should be a better balance between the tax paid by the middle class-business men, professionals and others-and the wealthier classes, corporations, etc.
There is also another problem, the partiality for the C.B.C. which has been criticiezd by many members on all sides of the House for many years. We are proud to be able to say that in Canada we enjoy freedom of the press, but a good many people seem to think that in the name of freedom anything goes. It has been said that our freedom begins where that of the other ends. It has also been asserted that freedom consisted in abiding by the law.
In my opinion, our bill of rights should state once and for all and for the benefit of the public at large, what is freedom. Are we deprived of our freedom when those who want to read or to make some research in libraries are required to abide by the rule?
Let us deal now with the problem of unemployment. What about some of our fellow-citizens over forty who
The Address-Mr. G. LeBlanc lose their job because of unfortunate and uncontrolable circumstances and who cannot find employment? At that age, most workers are still quite productive.
As regards unemployment, I think a useful method would be to make every effort to offer a wide variety of suggestions to our youth.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Young graduates are looking only for interesting and remunerating employment. But it would not be exaggerated, I think, to remind them that, on leaving school at 18 or 19, they can be ready, in a relatively short lap of time, to create jobs in small undertakings or businesses.
Regional development is a problem of particular interest to my friends in the Gaspe region and the Lower St. Lawrence, where is located the Rimouski constituency which I represent. For many years now, governments have spent millions of dollars to set up a program and my electors are becoming more and more concerned in that regard. They want to know if they have not been misled and when they will be able to see concrete achievements.
I am referring here to a measure taken in my riding, about which my fellow-citizens and myself feel proud: the creation of an inter-municipal committee for the Rimouski-Mont-Joli-Price zone. This initiative was taken by our own people, by citizens who think the government can help them, but who also believe that they must begin by helping themselves.
With regard to the projects of this inter-municipal committee, I hope that, in the fields coming under its jurisdiction, the federal government will give serious consideration to the requests of the members of this committee with regard to the improvement of the airport of this urban centre, and of the port of Rimouski, a very important port, to the creation of an industrial park and to improving both ocean and river shipping.
I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to the policy of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in connection with the building of low-cost housing. Back home low-cost housing units are being built as everywhere else in Canada but, although our directors, the officers of the Corporation, mean well, they have lost sight of the fact that what is a low price in Toronto, or Montreal is not so in our area, as when we speak of low-cost housing, the price must bear some relation to the salary scale prevailing in this particular area.
So, either the cost of housing remains at the same level with the possibility of increasing wages, or what would be even better from certain points of view, the price of those supposedly low-cost dwellings is reduced, so long as my fellow citizens obtain what they require.
I also have in mind a certain policy of the Canadian National Railways in regard to our region. I am thinking about the fate of some employees of this company, while everybody is talking about the protection of workers. I am one of them, as are most of the members of the House. I know that a man who has been employed by the company for one or two months perhaps must sleep in

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Marshall
his car because the company does not provide him with a place to live or does not pay his expenses.
I have in mind some investigation methods it uses to discuss...

I thank my hon. colleagues for giving me this permission. I will not exceed my time and I shall finish my speech as quickly as possible.
There are many other points which I would have liked to deal with. I might be able to come back to them. I would have liked to refer to in particular, the problem of the farmers and the producers of industrial milk which are of prime concern to us.
Before closing I should like to say again that, like several of my colleagues, I sincerely and earnestly support the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne because this speech gives us an image of the just society. I cannot understand why anyone could object to our desire that justice prevail among our people.
In addition, if we consider as a whole the three Speeches from the Throne since 1968, we notice that the last one is a consistent follow-up of the other two, with regard to the establishment of the just society. The second Speech from the Throne set up a program for drafting white papers for the purpose of establishing the structure or the framework of that society which the government wants to create in order to prepare, for our young people, and for all our fellow citizens, the Canada of the 80s or of the year 2000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The answers have been in front of the government's noses for years. The Economic Council of Canada had the answer over four years ago. They proved after countless reviews and studies, conferences and reports, that poverty was real. The Canadian Welfare Council and other Canadian organizations have produced answers on poverty. We are all aware that the Senate Committee on Poverty has travelled across Canada and produced answers. Now we are to have a nutritional study across Canada. And do you know what this committee is going to find out, Mr. Speaker? It will find out that poor people need more food which contains the correct vitamins. The government will study this report and print it in two official languages for the committee: the bodies of some 4 million Canadians will continue to deteriorate while this government continues to procrastinate.
Let me give you some examples of poverty, Mr. Speaker, as I have found it while touring the remote areas of my constituency. Picture if you will, Mr. Speaker, a Canadian citizen, bedridden for years in a room just large enough for himself and his wife who sits in a chair for hours and days on end without sleep because she does not have a bed to sleep in, and the room is only granted by the good graces of the family that has taken them in. Picture an elderly citizen with a mechanical heart, miles from a hospital and existing only by the grace of God, or imagine my dismay when I visited a family of six living on a meagre allowance and saw two invalid children suffering from chalk-bone, and our regulations restrict the special care required; how about the old age pensioner who wrote to me recently wondering why he has to pay back some of the $240 he earned last year selling newspapers to supplement his income.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I could mention many cases of people going blind because they cannot afford the necessary periodical corrective care or the cost of transportation to visit the proper care centre. This is not to mention the hundreds of families in remote areas who cannot afford decent accommodation and are living in shelters that you wouldn't believe. And yet this government and its experts hide their heads in the sand and brag about what they are doing about overcoming the housing problems in the cities. Does anyone ever hear of what they are doing to meet the housing requirements of those in the rural communities, or to provide the necessary water and sewage facilities? No, Mr. Speaker. They are going to wait until 1980, when they believe, in what can only be termed gross ignorance, that all the people in Canada will be moving to the larger centres. What hypocrisy!
I think it is time, Mr. Speaker, that we substituted a little human consideration and feeling for scientific studies. Here we are, in our concern for pollution, prepared to spend billions of dollars to control and prevent the pollution of the environment and we hesitate to spend money which is long past due to prevent the pollution of the bodies of millions of incapacitated Canadians both young and old. We continue to spend millions on medical research to prevent sickness and to learn the reasons for
The Address-Mr. Marshall
death by disease, yet we will not provide the moneys needed to prevent undernourishment of the bodies of the poor when we are so well aware of the cure. No, Mr. Speaker, the answer is not in more studies; the answer is in concern for our fellow man-and the sooner the better.
What about our youth in the remote areas of Canada? If we want a better Canada in the future and a better Canadian, we should be concentrating on providing a program of development for all the youth of Canada, and not just for the chosen few who happen to be living in the larger cities. We need a nationwide youth development program with proper guidance and leadership interwoven with our school systems in every nook and cranny in this country. I ask myself this question: Why is so little attention given to youth development and recreation in our list of priorities, when this is the basis of producing a better citizen and of finding in the future the better Canada for which we are looking? Again, we have reports, Mr. Speaker, the P. S. Ross report and the Harry Jerome projects; and the government expects to produce results with a $5 million Canada-wide physical fitness program. What we need, along with the new ministers of state, is a minister of youth development. Let us allocate money out of our budget in this direction. The return in champions and better citizens in the not-too-distant future would be amazing.
In my district of Humber-St. Georges-St. Barbe, Mr. Speaker, I have become well aware of those problems which can only be solved by properly thought-out and programmed development. The process can only evolve around the development of our natural resources. We have found, to our sorrow, that the basis of our economy for many years-the cod fishery-is being fast depleted. The minister is well aware of the problems in this area. While I realize that the problem is a delicate one from the point of view of enforcing restrictions to protect our fishing zones, I am convinced that the present minister is doing all he can to overcome the weaknesses of past governments in coping with these difficulties. I hope he will make progress in continuing liaison with foreign countries to respect the exclusiveness of our waters and at the same time provide that protection which is required to keep foreign draggers away from our Newfoundland shores, so that our people can survive against the deliberate raping of their livelihood.
I commend the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) for his efforts in that portfolio, but I hope he can do more to convince some of those in other closely associated departments that more assistance is required in the way of fisheries improvement loans and in the provision of better facilities to enable the fishermen to cope with new methods which are being introduced and to take advantage of the other species of fish which have been found, with success, through the development branch of his department. I hope, too, that he will look with favour upon my private member's motion which would make available subsidies to fishermen so they could provide themselves facilities which are vital to their success in this fast-changing industry. I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) announce that

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Marshall
more funds will be directed in order to assist in this area. I hope too, Mr. Speaker, that we will see during this session the promised catch insurance plan for fishermen and that it will be ready with the bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, on regional economic expansion. In my opinion, as I have stated many times in this House and in my province, this department could be the answer to the problems of the regionally despaired if, indeed, the plan were carefully studied, thought-out and programmed to achieve its aims and objectives. While I am more familiar with the plan from the viewpoint of Newfoundland, and especially my district, I am very disappointed due to the fact that the plan is going the way of the FRED program, which was studied for some years and scrapped here in Ottawa as being unacceptable in the form in which it was presented. I have to say that while the new development plan that is now being studied shows signs of better organization, the first phase of the plan as announced some months ago, and the projects approved, again show a lack of carefully thought-out, projected aims and a lack of intergovernmental co-operation.
To give a glaring example of one project I quote the case of the potential industrial development of Stephen-ville where, through the good graces of the American government, the province was handed over a modern complex of real estate, worth millions of dollars, which lends itself to a ready-made industrial park. The establishment of a liner board mill was supported by grants and loans under the federal department to support the industry with water and sewage systems, new roads, bridges and a high school. But there was the glaring, fundamental omission of common sense, fundamental plann'ng. The mill, which already employs over 200 people in the construction stage, was responsible for bringing in people from surrounding areas under relocation and has already created for the town of Stephenville a housing problem with which it cannot cope.
Eventually, when the mill goes into production it will employ some 700 people. By simple mathematics, Mr. Speaker, if you multiply 700 by a conservative figure of three per family, you will have some 2,000 human beings who will require housing. There will be the associated need for water and sewage, schools for the children, recreational facilities and other services which should have been foreseen from the outset. But instead, the town of Stephenville and the school authorities already cannot cope with the problem and there is a need for emergency measures to be taken, which can only result in extreme difficulty and eventual chaos. This is not only unfair to the local authorities but it is downright stupid fundamental planning by the supposed experts who are falling all over themselves in offices instead of listening and paying attention to the briefs which have been submitted by interested citizen organizations. It makes me wonder how sincere are the minister's words when he keeps repeating the now empty phrase that no development plan will be successful unless grass roots organizations become involved in the creation of a development plan.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I point out these facts to the minister, not for the sake of criticism but to emphasize that he has the co-operation of every organization in my district. They have listened, and want to participate for the good of their own community or area. I hope that every brief submitted by organizations from my district will be given the courtesy of consideration. I am prepared to give the benefit of the doubt and assume that the new senior appointments to the staff of the Department of Community and Social Development in the province will give that consideration.
The Regional Development Incentives Act as it applies to Newfoundland is almost a lost cause, Mr. Speaker, because it completely misses its objectives in so far as that province is concerned. The reason for this was given by the minister when he stated that it excludes some areas from types of activity such as the development of natural resources, which in some regions is the main, if not the only, source of development. Another bad feature is that it fails to provide assistance to those who want to expand small industry, through lack of capital. One example is a fish plant operator who was denied a grant because of some technicality of commitment. The applicant, who was expanding his fish operation, had to order new equipment from Germany six months in advance in order to get it in time for the fall herring season. He was turned down because he had made the commitment beforehand. Another example is that of an electrical plant operator who almost daily must refuse contracts because of lack of capital for expansion. The act should be flexible in order to give special consideration to those in regionally despaired areas who require more help than the industrial giants who will not come to Newfoundland when they can locate more centrally in Canada.
I cannot blame the federal government for not being willing to provide the funds for the development of a national park in my district. I sincerely hope that the government member from my province, a member of the cabinet, will do his utmost to convince the provincial government to turn over the necessary land to create the Bonne Bay Park, which will give an effective impetus to the economy of the province.
The need for public services induces me to make a plea to the new minister responsible for the Post Office. I was pleased to hear that the closing of post offices will halt and that the situation will be reviewed. The post offices in isolated communities of Newfoundland are still an important communications link, even in this day of satellites. I welcome the announcement. Another important item which should be reviewed is the salaries of postmasters in many communities. These salaries are, to say the least, shameful. I hope these salary scales will be reviewed as quickly as possible.
Still on the subject of communications, Mr. Speaker, there is a breakdown between the responsible federal department and the provincial government of Newfoundland. While I commend the CNT for the expansion program to extend telephones to the northwestern peninsula in my district, there are two failings. One is that the provincial government have failed to provide

October 13, 1970

the related power facilities, thus denying many communities this much needed telephone service. The other matter which has been forgotten is the cost to the consumer. Already one community has had all its telephones disconnected because the residents cannot afford to pay the charge. Is this good planning, Mr. Speaker? Is this equality?
I have reviewed the 68 measures mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I hope they will not be taken in the order in which they appear in the list. I sincerely hope that legislation relating to income security, veterans' pension legislation and the bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act will receive immediate consideration in this House. There is a fundamental military lesson which can be applied and of which the government should take note. An advancing army can progress only as fast as its slowest elements, and after success in reaching an objective it should consolidate its position before advancing further. I say to this government that our aims in science and technology are running away with us. We cannot cope with the situation. We have already discovered that all the wealth we have gathered will be of no avail because we will have to spend it to control and prevent pollution.
We must consolidate our position. Our wealth in resources has been in the ground and in the sea for hundreds of years. It will still be there in a few years hence. We should look over our shoulders and raise the standard of living of those who lag behind and are unable to catch up without our help. This is our duty and responsibility as a state. Each day we delay, we must remember in our conscience that we are responsible for bringing closer to death those who are incapacitated, maimed and whose bodies are deteriorating because we are not living up to our responsibility. We must concentrate immediately on helping the aged, sick, maimed, incapacitated, blind, deaf and retarded. This is our duty as a state. We owe this to these citizens because they are unable to care for themselves. This is their equality of opportunity. I hope the government will direct their immediate attention to this part of our society, to give some meaning to their concern for the disadvantaged people and areas of our nation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, wish to add my congratulations to the mover and to the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Both these members have displayed their ableness in moving and seconding the Address in Reply.
I want to concentrate on the aspect of urban affairs in the few minutes available to me this afternoon. The riding which I represent is not considered an urban riding although a very small portion of the city of Calgary is located within it. I want to emphasize the importance of urban development to the small, growing communities of Canada rather than dwelling upon the importance of an urban affairs department for the burgeoning, large cities of this country.
All who have a concern for the direction of social and economic development in this country will welcome the
The Address-Mr. Sulatycky
announced intention of the government to designate a minister solely responsible for urban affairs and housing. The problems of the cities are well recognized by citizens of this country, whether they live in the cities or elsewhere. It is also recognized that the federal government is greatly inhibited by the Constitution from taking any firm and unilateral initiatives with regard to cities. Hopefully, all provinces will co-operate in any attempt by the national government to act in this area in which the provinces have the greater, and virtually exclusive, jurisdiction. While we await a redistribution of powers among the various governments in the country we will have to do the best with the system which exists at the present time. We do not do our best if we exclude the national government from an active role in urban policies. The new ministry will give it such an active role.
Fortunately, though we may have problems in our cities, they lack the severity of those faced by cities in the neighbouring country to our south or in other highly-industrialized and urbanized areas of the world. No less an observer than Buckminster Fuller has said, for example, that Toronto is a city without problems. All of our larger cities display in general a very attractive face, making them appealing to the visitor or to the residents. But behind this face are problems which will soon become insoluble if we do not quickly come to grips with them.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Solutions to the problems of our cities have been suggested by many who rank as experts in the field. It is a field which is perhaps best left to experts and I, for one, will not presume to offer my own solutions. My concern runs in another direction. Basically, it is that in attempting to develop cures for the ills of the city we do not lead to its further degeneration. We shall avoid this pitfall only by setting a clear course of action based on the conscious choice of the type of settlement pattern we wish to see. Do we wish to have only a dozen or so extremely large cities in which almost all of our population is concentrated or do we wish to have many cities of differing sizes offering our citizens the greatest choice? Do we wish our cities to be located only where large concentrations of people are found, or are there more desirable locations elsewhere?
The answers to these questions are already determined. If we do not make a conscious choice to the contrary, within a very short time most of our population will be living in the two dozen larger cities already established. The rapid influx of people may well prevent the solution of the ills which the cities now face, because we shall constantly be a step behind the growth of the population.
If we are to design a sensible system of settlement in Canada we must first discard two common Canadian characteristics. The first is the sense of inevitability associated with the growth of our larger urban centres. This is evident in our constant prognostications of population patterns in Canada ten or twenty years from now. It is displayed by those who announce that at a stated point in time a certain percentage of our people will be concentrated in only a few areas. It is shown, for exam-

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Sulatycky pie, in the statement by a Canadian trade magazine that such an influx-and I quote-"cannot be stopped any more than the ocean surf can be turned back". It is reinforced by civic politicians who make statements such as "this city has a certain momentum which it must maintain." Any more of such momentum is likely to lead to destruction.
The second characteristic of which we must cleanse ourselves is our "mining camp" psychology. In the development of human communities we have tended to concentrate our efforts on barely a handful of communities, establishing other settlements only temporarily to serve the interests of the dominant communities. This is a pattern which began with the earliest of Canadian industries, the fur trade and which still continues today. In the era of the fur trade many trading posts dotted the landscape, built only to serve immediate needs and having no other purpose than to satisfy the commercial interests of embryonic cities hundreds of thousands of miles distant. The pattern has repeated itself a number of times since then. Today, as we survey the landscape of Canada, we find that outside southern Ontario and the St. Lawrence Valley area there are fewer than ten major cities. Scattered about the country are hundreds of smaller communities. We find them wherever there is a mine, an oilfield, a pulp mill or another resource based industry. Some of these communities are as old as, or older than, the Canadian nation, and others are new having sprung to life only within the last few months or years.
Most often those that are old are struggling for survival, while those that are new are too blinded by hope and confidence in the future to envision themselves as tomorrow's Barkervilles and Belle Islands. Canadians are slow to recognize this very evident demographic characteristic. Even the government's task force on housing and urban development did not note it. Its only reference to the communities between those considered rural and those considered urban, said:
As a sort of half-way house between rural Canada and the burgeoning urban areas lie the small communities which dot the landscape, particularly across the prairies. They are a mixed bag. In regions where agriculture is strong, one finds prosperous and growing service communities meeting the needs of the surrounding population, generating a growth factor of their own and seemingly on the verge, in a few cases at least, of that "great leap forward" into full urban status. In areas where the rural economy is weak, so are the towns, many of them struggling with local industries of varying relevance to ensure that a baby born or a new resident acquired is a net population gain and not merely an offsetting factor against the drain to the city.
This is not an accurate picture of the pattern of settlement in Canada. Our settlements are not concentrated only in the large cities and in farming areas. There are many communities which do not rely solely on agriculture, settlements which do have an industrial base, narrow though it may be, and which are capable of sustained growth if they are given a chance and not forced to compete unfairly with the large urban centres of this country.
Our mining camp psychology is at the core of regional economic disparity in this country. Many of the areas which suffer from a weak economy do so because of their
reliance on a single industry which is no longer viable. What I recommend is that in dealing with urban affairs we should devote all our efforts to developing as many urban communities as possible, the greatest attention being given to the sound economic development of the smaller towns and cities which show a potential for urbanization. Some very eminent people are making similar proposals. Earlier this year the United States Secretary of Agriculture, Clifford M. Harding, called for national policies specifically designed to bring about unprecedented growth in rural areas. He advocated the creation in and around the smaller cities and towns of "sufficiently good employment opportunities and living environments that larger and larger numbers of families may choose to rear their children there."
Throughout Canada there are many small towns and cities which are well suited to sustain a larger population. Some of them are growing, others are not. The one certain thing is that in the absence of a changed attitude on the part of governments in Canada, and Canadians, these communities will all gradually decline because of the present overwhelming trend to concentrate all our economic activity in the largest centres.
The difficulties which these communities face in maintaining their growth are similar to those faced by others in their situation wherever they might be in Canada. I am sure this applies to such communities in my own riding of Rocky Mountain, communities which, as a matter of fact, are among the fastest growing in the country. Grand Cache, for example, in the northern end of the constituency is Canada's newest community, having been built only in the last two years to serve the huge coal mining developments associated with the Mcln-tyre-Porcupine Mines near the Smokey River. A number of other communities in the riding have doubled or even tripled their population in the last ten years. Among the growing communities of western Alberta are Fox Creek, Whitecourt, Drayton Valley, Edson, Hinton, Canmore, Black Diamond and the communities which comprise the Crowsnest Pass region. As I say, the problems which face these communities are similar to those confronting any small growing community wherever it is situated in Canada. The basic difficulty is that they must compete with the large cities for capital, labour and industry. This is the unfairest competition imaginable. The small community always comes out second best.
While there is a drastic need for housing in the large cities, there is also a similar need in the small centre which is growing. But the sources from which a person may obtain capital for constructing housing are very much more limited in the small community. Indeed, often it is impossible to get financing for housing in many towns. In large cities there are many branches of chartered banks, various trust companies and usually a wide selection of mortgage companies with which a developer or an individual may arrange financing for housing projects. In the average town, there may be one or two, perhaps three, branches of chartered banks, and often they are reluctant to make housing loans except for single family dwellings.

October 13, 1970

[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
As in the cities, there is demand for various types of accommodation in smaller centres also, but the financing of such accommodation is very, very difficult to obtain. In many communities only the banks and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will finance housing of any sort. It is also evident there are more CMHC programs available for cities than for smaller centres.
If one should try to borrow money for a housing development from a trust company or life insurance company, for example, one is given the cold shoulder. A number of months ago I had an opportunity to see just how much the cards are stacked against the growth of smaller centres. A person who was interested in developing a number of housing emits in a town in my riding invited me to attend with him at the office of a major Canadian mortgage corporation in Edmonton. We were invited into the mortgage manager's office and he proceeded to tell us that his firm had vast amounts of money available for investment and housing purposes. He displayed a very lively interest in the project as it was described to him by my constituent, who saved to the end the fact that this particular project happened to be in a town of some 3,000 people situated some miles outside the city. When this fact was made known to the manager, his attitude changed remarkably and he simply stated that no funds were available for mortgages outside the city.
This is not an isolated instance. I have experienced similar examples during my law practice in rural areas of Alberta. It is a very common occurrence for financing for very worth-while projects to be refused simply because the projects are situated in a community that is not one of the major urban areas of Canada.
The problem of providing housing to growing small communities appears to prevail throughout Canada. A Calgary firm, Atco Industries, has had a great deal of experience in providing prefabricated housing for resource communities, not only in Canada but throughout the world. In an article written in January of last year the president of that firm, Mr. R. D. Southern, said the following:
While the problems of providing low cost acceptable housing to isolated and urban areas are largely similar, one major difference precludes any sensible plan for providing housing to the population presently moving into and required for industrialization and expansion of Canada's isolated northern regions. That problem is an almost complete lack of ability to provide mortgaging for normal residential purchases. This inability is not hard to understand, when the sparseness of population and vastness of the isolated regions are considered, but it also extends to the small towns that are the nucleus of northern and isolated area growth.
It is incongruous, in a country like Canada, which has been and should be committed to the industrialization and expansion of its northern territoriesand, I might add, other areas capable of sustaining economic growth-
__for the future economic benefit of all Canadians, that rather
than providing incentives to locate in these areas, there is a complete and devastating road block to the provision of a dignified class of housing.
The Address-Mr. Sulatycky
I should like to emphasize the last statement, that there is a complete and devastating roadblock to the provision of a dignified class of housing in these small communities. This extends not only to housing; these communities run into difficulty in arranging financing for such things as services, the ordinary requirements of any community. As well, businesses have difficulty in arranging financing for commercial expansion. I believe this applies equally to growing small communities in other parts of Canada as well as to communities in northern Canada.
As I said, the problem does not stop at housing; in the area of commercial development availability of financing is just as critical. I have had many businessmen in a number of small communities tell me that they have run into obstacle after obstacle in attempting to obtain capital for expansion purposes. Other businessmen in large cities have the necessary capital made readily available to them, but it seems that when a small town entrepreneur comes to draw from the well, it suddenly runs dry.
These are problems that we must solve soon. In solving them we may very well help to solve some of the problems in the large cities. But we will not solve them by letting current economic and technological advances take their own course. It is certain that the end result of that course will be a greater and greater concentration of population in fewer and fewer locations. I do not think this is necessary or desirable. It is certainly not inevitable.
I find comfort in the words of the distinguished American public servant, John W. Gardner, who served as secretary of health, education and welfare in President Johnson's administration in 1965. Before I refer to his comments, Mr. Speaker, perhaps this would be a good opportunity to call it six o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we rose for dinner I was saying that it is neither inevitable nor desirable that all, or even an extremely large portion, of our population be crowded into only the very largest cities. I was about to quote the words of John W. Gardner, former United States secretary of health, education and welfare, who said:
Within the past 20 years the urge on the part of large numbers of people to pile into cities has become anachronistic. For ten thousand years people had excellent reason to crowd them-
94

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. Sulatycky
selves into cities. Only there could they find the richness and variety of stimulation that make for creativity, the massed resources and economies of scale that make possible the greatest enterprises. But today, thanks to advances in communication, transportation and the arts of organization, we can provide these conditions at any point on the map that strikes our fancy. So the questions become: How can we best use land space? What patterns of settlement and open space best serve our purposes? How can we revitalize rural areas, create new cities, and overhaul existing cities in ways that serve human needs, the requirements of economic vitality and the claims of beauty?
The answer to these questions is certainly not by crowding more and more people into the largest cities. One further observation which one can make from viewing the developments of urbanization in the United States is that although more and more people crowd into and around the cities, fewer and fewer people wish to live there. In a Gallup poll taken last year it was found that most Americans would live in a small town or on a farm if they had their choice. Only 18 per cent really desired to live in cities.
In Canada we have the opportunity to create for our people the greatest variety of living environments. That should be the prime objective of the new ministry of urban affairs. To reach it we will have to devise acceptable means for influencing the location of economic activity. We should not hesitate, if necessary, to conscript capital for this purpose. There is no doubt that government alone cannot provide all the funds necessary for this purpose. If our existing financial institutions fail to meet the needs and the demands of growth in smaller centres, mechanisms must be developed to compel these institutions to apportion some of their available resources to such communities. I would say that if the same institutions fail to meet the needs of the larger cities, we should not hesitate to compel them to apply their resources in ways which are of the greatest benefit in the opinion of the people of the country rather than in the opinion of the directors of the corporations alone. These funds should not be limited to housing and to industrial activity but should provide capital for industrial expansion and commercial expansion as well as for the services usually required in municipalities.
Any program that will improve our large cities will succeed only if it is tied to a program to increase the over-all number of cities in this country. We must ensure that we have not only a number of very large cities but that we have many small cities-small, but lively and thriving-spread throughout the country. I suggest this is the direction which must be followed if we are to succeed in any urban policy in this country.
In summation, I should like to refer again to the points I have attempted to make. I believe one of the tasks of the ministry of urban affairs should be to take an inventory of existing communities in Canada to determine which are capable of sustaining public growth and to ensure that these communities do not suffer because of increased emphasis being placed on the larger cities. I believe we should ensure that capital for housing, commercial and industrial development is made available to the smaller as well as to the larger centres. Only then, I believe, will we develop a sound system of geographic

development in this country and a sound settlement pattern providing for the people of Canada the opportunities which this land should make available to them.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to extend my sincere congratulations to the movers of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne (Messrs. A. B. Douglas and Trudel). They performed their tasks extremely well.
This debate is giving me and other hon. members a chance to criticize the present government for its lack of decision and imagination when it comes to meeting its obligations. This debate enables me also to let the proper authorities know of the conditions prevailing in my constituency and of the needs of my constituents.
Taking into account the promises made to them during the 1968 election campaign, Canadians were justified in believing that a Liberal government would offer them favourable conditions in all fields, and would solve problems quickly and completely.
However, even a brief examination or hasty review, of present conditions will show that the problems are still numerous. While they pile up one on top of the other, the government fails sadly in its obligations and does nothing to solve them.
Thus, I am not telling anybody anything when I say that inflation is still solidly established, that taxes have never been so high, that the present rate of unemployment is very high, that thousands of householders cannot earn a living for their families and that our industries, especially the textile and shoe industries, operate at a slow-down rate, when they are not completely closed, while imports increase at a frightening rhythm.
According to data from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the gross national product increased only by 1 per cent during the second half of the current year. For the first six months of the year, the number of dwelling units started was 40 per cent lower than last year.
From January to June new car sales were 15 per cent lower than for the same period last year and there were 75 per cent more bankruptcies.
This is in short where the Liberal government has led the country in return for the confidence the people put in it at the 1968 elections.
Mr. Speaker, since the present debate began, some Liberal members have accused the official opposition of obstructing the legislation proposed in the field of agriculture to help that deserving group of our society. They mentioned Bill C-196 and Bill C-197, blaming the opposition and particularly the official opposition for systematic obstruction.
We are conscious of having done our duty in this field as well as in others, and of having acted in the best interest of the farmers.
If we had accepted Bills C-196 and C-197 as they were introduced, the Canadian farmers would have been embarrassed by these two measures since, in both cases,
October 13, 1970

many amendments have been proposed then rejected by this government. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has never agreed to take into account the views of the opposition. All he wanted was to have the House approve these bills as introduced and they were so flawed that we thought it our duty to delay their passage as long as possible, mainly that of Bill C-197, to help the population and particularly the farmers.
Our attitude in this field has been identical to that we had regarding the White Paper presented, some time ago, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). Had we heeded him, we would have passed the legislation sponsored by him as it was, whereas today a joint committee of the Commons and the Senate has adopted a great many of our views on fiscal reform.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, far from seeking to create obstruction, we have had as our sole purpose to see that the people of Canada get the legislation they deserve.
Returning to Bill C-197, Mr. Speaker, when speaking to farmers we realize that those the legislation would most affect know very little about it. Few of them are aware that the council responsible for applying the legislation would be fully government-appointed. The farmers expect that they will have their say in an area which concerns them so closely. In fact, I think that those on the front benches opposite have missed the chance to tell the farmers, for instance, that the Council, entirely appointed by the government, and not elected as we want it to be, would control quotas, marketing, storage, labeling and distribution and would have the right to collect charges from the farmers.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
They are completely unaware of that. Ministers should therefore go to the province of Quebec and clearly explain this provision of the law. They would realize that farmers have a lot of objections.
Mr. Speaker, within the few minutes left to me I would like to particularly call the hon. members' attention on the conditions prevailing more especially in my constituency. Needless to say that the city of St. Hyacinthe is considered as a natural centre of culture and regional attractions. Over there, farmers and factory workers are familiar with each other and there is complete agreement between these two groups of our society.
Of course, my riding is affected as much as any other by the general conditions prevailing in Canada at the present time. However, the city of Saint-Hyacinthe being a textile centre, the problems of that particular industry affect especially the workers of my riding.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time that I have had occasion to speak about this matter here in the House. Since the present government has been in power, I have taken every opportunity to point out to the responsible minister, and the government as a whole, that some action was urgently required in order to maintain this industry in our area.
Unfortunately, all my requests fell into deaf ears with the result that today our textile workers wonder how long they will be able to keep their jobs.
The Address-Mr. Ricard
The textile industry deserves the attention of this government. It provides work for at least 83,000 people, 47,000 of whom live in the province of Quebec. Its yearly output in my province is estimated at $850 million. Every year several millions of dollars are invested in equipment and in the construction or renovation of buildings.
In spite of the importance of this industry, this government has waited until it is almost too late to take the necessary action.
We have warned the government, particularly about the field of shirt making, that imports were much too heavy for the Canadian industry to feel at ease. Nothing was done, except after the damage was irreparable. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did take some action, but it was too late. The harm was done.
In St. Hyacinthe, for instance, the Yamaska Shirt which once had 350 employees cut its staff by 75 per cent. In factories such as Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company and Penman's Limited which employed hundreds of workers a few years ago, there are much less now.
As far as the footwear industry is concerned, official statistics show that since 1963, 45 manufacturers have gone out of business. Some industries are getting ready to reduce the number of employees or to close down.
In 1960, there were 249 Canadian plants in the footwear industry, while in 1970, there are only 189 shoe manufacturers in the country. In 1966, there were 25,360 employees while, in 1970, there were only 22,000.
On the other hand, shoe imports in 1956 amounted to 6,898,315 pairs as compared with 46,100,000 pairs in 1969.
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the government trading with underdeveloped countries, but I believe our first responsibility is to ensure employment for Canadians before throwing our doors wide open to imports.
Last week I had the opportunity to go into a shoe shop in Saint-Hyacinthe, and in talking with the owner I found to my amazement that 80 per cent of his inventory was imported.
It means that the Canadian market-and the other stores are identical to that one-supplies only 20 per cent of the domestic consumption. That is an anomaly when one knows that workers, in the Canadian shoe industry are amply equipped and able to make a product that will meet the needs of Canadians.
Canadian footwear can favourably compare with any other. However, in certain government quarters, it is suggested that if we favour imports on so large a scale, it is because we want the protection of the Canadian consumer.
Mr. Speaker, in the light of my personal experience, even with the wave of shoe imports from foreign countries, far from paying less for my shoes in 1970, I have to pay more than when the Canadian market was supplied mostly by Canadian plants.
This argument does not hold and before making people believe that we want to protect them, it would be better to take the necessary steps to protect Canadian workers.
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to discuss many other subjects, but since time goes by and that I have only a
23226-'n

October 13, 1970
The Address-Mr. M. Lessard
few minutes left, I would like to discuss the measure concerning designated areas.
The area of Saint-Hyacinthe has all the essential criteria in order to be declared a designated area. On many occasions, I have made to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) personal representations which have been followed by those of the city council and trade unions of the city of Saint-Hyacinthe. Unfortunately, they have not been taken into consideration.
That attitude, I am sorry to say, induces the people back home to think that the riding is not being treated fairly.
I say it again: the Saint-Hyacinthe area has all the criteria required to be recognized as a designated area. At least 20 per cent of the work force is unemployed. All these things have been pointed out to the responsible minister, delegations have come here to meet him; but justice has been denied the area of Saint-Hyacinthe. I do not hesitate to say so, this is injustice, even gross injustice towards the people of Saint-Hyacinthe. It is injustices of that kind that breed the events we have witnessed in the province of Quebec in the last few days. Such injustices give certain elements of the population springboards from which to demonstrate and attack the government.
Once again. I urge the government to eradicate those injustices because they are detrimental to mutual understanding and national unity.
Mr. Speaker, those were the remarks I wanted to make. I trust they will be taken into serious consideration, this in the best interest of the electors of my riding.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
